subtopic: COMMUNICATIONS AND CULTURE-FOURTEENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
COMMUNICATIONS AND CULTURE-FOURTEENTH REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 96(2), I have the honour to present the fourteenth report of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture in both official languages.
This report addresses itself to the issue of taxation of the artists and the arts. The key recommendation of our report aims to give force of law to a definition of the professional status of artists which, along with six other recommendations, would allow the artists and related organizations to receive more equitable treatment under Canada's tax laws. While the committee members accept that the principle of tax fairness was adopted in the White Paper on tax reform, we as committee members also accept that there are special circumstances to which different groups of taxpayers may be subject. In this case we believe that the arts should be considered, given the special nature of artists and the arts in Canada today.
Our seven recommendations are fair suggestions and represent long expressed needs of Canadian artists. It is our hope that the Government will consider these recommendations for implementation.

The Committee therefore requests that the government produce a reply to this report in accordance with Standing Order 99(2).
I take this opportunity to thank the representatives of all three parties for their care in writing this unanimous report with a really parliamentary spirit.
[Editor's Note: See today's Votes and Proceedings.]

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 106, I have the honour and the privilege to present a number of petitions signed by residents of Atikokan and the surrounding area. The signatures number over 200 in this case. The petition is about the northern residents' tax deduction. The residents of Atikokan believe that in its present form it is discriminatory because many communities not on the list are adjacent to listed communities. The Township of Atikokan in particular and its surrounding area was excluded from the designated area only because it is located too close to Thunder Bay.
The petitioners argue that the listed communities and many of those communities left off the list share identical environments in that they are northern, isolated communities paying increased costs for food, fuel and housing, and that the tax deduction was designed to assist in alleviating the added costs involved with living in northern, isolated communities.
The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to declare the Township of Atikokan and the surrounding area to be eligible for the northern residents' deduction.

subsubtopic: PROTECTION OF RIGHTS OF THE UNBORN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the duty and responsibility to present this petition on behalf of constituents throughout the riding of Fraser Valley West. The nature of this petition is to express concern over the total lack of legal control over abortions in Canada today. The purpose of this petition is to call on Parliament to implement laws to protect the unborn child.
The petitioners state that all human beings are deserving of legal protection and that the unborn child is a human being and in need of preservation from the moment of origin; namely, the time of conception. Furthermore, the people who have signed this document are particularly concerned that at the present time, there is no law to defend the unborn from being destroyed in the womb. These constituents pray that the Members of this House will implement legislation to protect the unborn.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Hawkes (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, question No. 279 will be answered today.

During the past year, have studies been undertaken by the government concerning the depletion of the ozone layer in the atmosphere and remedial measures in respect thereof and, if so, in each case (a) by what organization or individual (b) under what terms of reference?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Yes. The following studies are being undertaken by Environment Canada under the terms of reference outlined by the Montreal Protocol (signed in September 1987) on substances that deplete the ozone layer:
-a control options report which will identify the choices available to meet the obligations set out in the Montreal Protocol;
-development of a comprehensive information base to evaluate the costs and benefits associated with each identified control option; and
-in-house studies to identify the 1986 Canadian consumption of controlled substances in order to establish Canadian reduction targets.
Environment Canada is also involved in:
-studies concerning the chemical composition of the stratosphere with particular emphasis on implications for the Canadian Arctic; and
-global studies aimed at determining levels of ozone layer depletion from ground based and satellite borne instruments.

The House resumed from Friday, April 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. McMillan that Bill C-30, an Act to amend the National Parks Act and to amend an Act to amend the National Parks Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and the motion of Mr. Hawkes:
That the question be now put.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that the country is anxious to have this legislation passed, and I certainly do not want to delay its passage, but as the Member for Bow River, a riding which includes Lake Louise and Banff, I feel that there is some responsibility on my part to say a few words in connection with this very important legislation.
First, I would like to pay a tribute to the Minister, who has been willing to discuss various aspects of the Act with the people of Banff National Park and with Members who are concerned about preserving the beauty of our national parks. The Minister has been very tolerant and very free to discuss these many items, and I look forward to further discussions when the Bill goes to committee.
I would like to say a word about two or three items that are of very great concern to the people I represent. The first deals with the Banff air strip. When it comes to development, certainly no one to whom I have spoken in the Banff area or in the Alberta caucus has any notion of putting in place something like a Coney Island in our national parks. That would be the furthest thing from our thoughts. We want to preserve this beauty, but we want to make the beauty available to as many Canadians and as many people of the world as possible. I believe that that is in keeping with the spirit of the National Parks Act.
Certainly there is no thought of having a Coney Island, but an air strip would not destroy any property. It is already there. The air strip has been there for about 20 years. To my knowledge, there has never been one accident in connection with this air strip during that entire time.
Banff, as everyone knows, is the mid-way point between Springbank and Golden. It is critical that pilots have the option to land in Banff if there is a sudden change in weather. The weather changes very rapidly in this area and many times, as a matter of fact on an average of four times a month, airplanes have to land in order to avoid terrible accidents. This is because the Bow Corridor is the main VFR route through the Rockies, and I must emphasize that: the Bow Corridor is the main VFR route through the Rockies. An average of 10 transmitting aircraft go through there every day.
I mentioned before that this air strip would not interfere with the environment or with the animals. As a matter of fact,
National Parks Act
the elk have prospered and thrived in this very area throughout the years. If we want to deal with animals that are not quite so desirable, the gophers have even done well on the air strip. There is no thought of interfering with the environment, but we are living in the 20th century and air strips are necessary in these places. Certainly the air strip in this area aids the cause of safety.
Many times, those who live in Banff have used their aircraft for searches for those who have been lost, particularly in the winter time. This area in the winter-time is inhabited by elk and these elk have done well. There has never been an accident and they have thrived in this area.
I would like to urge the Hon. Minister to consider the retention of this air strip in the Banff National Park. I believe it is essential not only for the aircraft but for safety as well.
I would like to deal now with one or two points in connection with development in the area. I do not know how many Hon. Members have had to drive all night to find a place to sleep in Banff National Park, but I have. In the summer-time particularly it is very difficult to find accommodation. When you consider that more than a million people, Canadians and others from around the world, go to the park every year, it would leave a very sour taste in the mouths of those who cannot find a place to sleep. There is also a need for good eating places. These I think add lustre to the park and our enjoyment of it. Without a place to sleep or eat no one is going to enjoy a holiday in Banff or anywhere else. So when we talk about reasonable development in the area, we are certainly not talking about Coney Island type development. We are simply asking that we have development so that Canadians are able to enjoy the beauties of the Banff National Park setting.
The same thing applies to the two ski areas, Sunshine and Lake Louise. They have to compete with ski areas in other parts of Canada and the U.S. If their equipment and facilities are not up to date, then we lose those people who would like to enjoy the beauties of the park and do their skiing. After all, enjoyment is not just in standing on Banff Avenue and gazing at Sulphur Mountain. Enjoyment is doing things in the national park in keeping with the park. Certainly skiing is one of those. Hundreds of people enjoy skiing, and development at Sunshine will simply make its facilities somewhat equal to those found in other ski areas. I have seen signs in the outskirts of Calgary urging skiers to go down to Montana and other parts of the U.S. This not only costs the people of Canada revenue, it makes it difficult for those operating the ski areas.
Lake Louise also wants to improve its facilities, which are not equal to what can be found elsewhere, and they want to put in a quad chair. This is not going to hurt the environment because it is being carried out between the main lodge and the top of the mountain. It will simply take people from one of the lower places to a higher location in order that they can enjoy the beauty and the skiing. The existing lift is certainly not

RCMP and public servants in Banff are dedicated people and should not be taxed on the amount of reduction they receive in their rents.
The other point I wish to mention briefly is that for over 20 years there have been trailers in the townsite of Lake Louise. People were required to buy a trailer in order to work for Parks Canada. There is now a move to have these people give up their homes, which are trailers, and become renters. I do not think that is sound. The trailers have been there for 20 years and are not hurting anyone. We should leave those trailers there for a few more years and the problem will solve itself. Let us not make these Canadian homeowners into renters. It is the philosophy of the Government that people should own their own homes. Here is a chance to put our words into practice.
In conclusion, Banff National Park is one of the beauty spots of the world. We want it to be there forever for Canadians to enjoy. However, we want it to be available to all types of Canadians- the old, the crippled, and the young-to come and enjoy the grandeur and the majesty of that beautiful place. I support the passage of this Bill and look forward to discussions on it in committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak today and of course to support Bill C-30 and to congratulate the Minister for bringing in some measures required to conserve the national parks.
At the same time, the need to amend this bill and to add the measures required for the proper and true protection of the great outdoors must be pointed out. This bill does not provide a clear definition of the areas of wilderness that must be protected for citizens of the future, native people and outdoor activities. This is a shortcoming of the bill under consideration today. In talking about the measures proposed by some Conservative Members and the Conservative Government, the need to properly protect the wilderness areas becomes quite obvious.

I am pleased to see this Bill before us. I hope that the Minister himself will speak on the Bill and will answer questions in the House about some of the measures which are not adequate. Perhaps he will put to rest some of the rumours about pressure in the Conservative caucus, especially in Alberta, to weaken the measures before us. The Bill before us is not a strong Bill. It is a very necessary Bill but has been weakened. We understand that a better Bill came out of the Ministry of the Environment but it has been weakened in the course.
One of the major deficiencies which I want to cite is the failure to include a clear definition of a wilderness area. The Bill will permit the Minister to establish wilderness areas but it does not say what they are. Aircraft are allowed to fly in
National Parks Act
wilderness areas, there can be rudimentary campsites and some kind of tourism will be permitted in them. There is pressure by Alberta Conservatives to see that there is more development in the parks.
It is very important when only 1.5 per cent of the land mass of Canada is consecrated to national parks, when the land that is protected is as small a part of our natural heritage as it is, that there be some substantial protection. This Bill does not go far enough toward doing that.
Alberta Conservatives want to see more development. They are afraid that condos cannot go up in a wilderness area. There is a corridor in the middle of Maligne Lake, supposedly a wilderness area, where boats can ply. There are houses and cottages at one end. What kind of a wilderness area is this?
The previous speaker spoke about the need to have tourism and to allow everyone to see a wilderness area. That is a contradiction. There is a place for tourism and a place for people to enjoy our national parks, but we must be very clear that it is fundamental for the survival of Canada that we have some real wilderness areas. This is part of our heritage and is for the protection of species. We do not have enough of that at present and there is a real risk that there will be further encroachments.
I think of the comments which have already been made about the ski areas. We do have some ski areas allowed in national parks and the proposal from some Conservative Members is that there ought to be more of them, that they ought to be expanded. We currently have five ski areas in national parks and a sixth is provided for by federal-provincial agreement in Newfoundland. The government policy is to limit development of ski areas but it has not been rigorously enforced.
The Minister has expressed his willingness to entertain changes to this section of Bill C-30. He says that it is all right if the committee studying the Bill decides to defer a decision on the Sunshine ski hill to some future date. Sunshine has been very adept at getting further developments permitted. It has people lobbying for it to have the policies bent. I am very leery of this and hope that the Minister will have a firm backbone on this issue.
Given that we only have a small area of Canada devoted to national parks, it is absolutely vital that there not be further encroachments. There is a place for commercial tourism but there is a place for Canada to stand firm about the protection of nature. That has to be a priority, and, as environment critic, I will certainly be firm about speaking strongly for those kinds of measures.
Bill C-30 will allow for boundaries to be established for municipal areas for Banff and Jasper. Two reasons that the Government has offered are to permit local self-government and to limit the development of town sites. However, we are

April 19, 1988
National Parks Act
not offered any idea of what these boundaries will be. They may go wider than what we would like and essentially be another way of reducing the areas that are really set aside for the survival of species in Canada.
Citizens of Jasper have already indicated that they do not want to pursue self-government at this time. Residents of Banff will vote later on whether or not they want to negotiate it. Before the committee begins its study of the Bill, the Government should bring forward its draft boundaries. We should know what we are passing. There should not be surprises later.
I have mentioned the role of the Alberta Government in lobbying on this measure. I want to refer specifically to some of the comments it has made. They show that the Alberta Government does not really understand what protection of the environment is all about.
On the question of ski areas, the document stating the views of the Alberta Government on the amendments to the National Parks Act states: "We cannot support the amendments which which seek to limit expansion of existing ski facilities and preclude new developments."
To continue: "Foreclosing the option of future ski development in Banff and Jasper National Parks would be a serious obstacle to expanding the tourism sector".
Yes, it would be. However, there are other places where there can be expansion of commercial skiing. That is a very legitimate activity and we support it, but the very raison d'etre of national parks is to preserve our natural heritage. Some things simply do not go together and the purpose of having national parks is to give a high priority to conservation and to ensure that at some point we say that making a buck is not the most important. We must show some responsibility for the future.
The Alberta Government points out that the boundaries for Banff and Jasper town sites, once fixed by act of Parliament, would require an act of Parliament to change the boundaries. It considers that unnecessary and cumbersome and wants flexibility. Why? It wants to allow for more commercial developments. In short, the Alberta Government wants to weaken the national parks system and take some of this out of the land bank for the future and devote it to making money commercially, something to which 99 per cent of Canada is already devoted. In short, it wants to weaken the whole idea of having a national parks system.
Let me continue to quote the brief of the Alberta Government: "There is a fundamental difference between Alberta's approach to land and resource management on public lands and the approach adopted by Parks Canada with the national parks".
Yes, there certainly is a difference. The approach taken by Parks Canada is the proper one. While I may argue that it is not strong enough in terms of conservation, and there are areas where I have some worries about it being the thin edge of the
wedge in terms of how it describes pollution and the kinds of developments that would be allowed, it is certainly far better than the approach proposed by the Alberta Government.
Let me turn to wilderness areas. The Alberta brief states: "We are concerned that the amendment might restrict present tourism related activities and exclude future development of appropriate tourism related facilities and activities which recognize the wilderness attributes of these areas".
One cannot have it both ways. If you really want to recognize the wilderness aspects, you cannot be having entertainment and recreation, more hotels and casinos with slot machines, dancing, parties and more fish and chip shops.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: There go the NDP Members exaggerating again. What nonsense.
It is quite clear in the part to which they want to add that recreation and entertainment areas would be permitted. Is this recreation and entertainment for the gophers, elk and caribou?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext: Ask Ian about skiing.

Skiing enterprises are quite appropriate, but not in national parks. There must be limitations on that. Some of the positive measures in the Bill include expanding national parks and incorporating in the legislation some decisions that have already been made and announced. Bill C-30 entrenches the establishment of Ellesmere Island National Park and makes provision for the establishment of the Grasslands National Park. Naturally, we support this.
The Minister also proposed that we could establish the first marine national park in the Bruce area through an amendment at committee. We certainly would support that, but wonder why it was not provided for in the original Bill since it is something the department has been considering for some time. The need to establish marine parks has certainly been agreed upon by environmentalists for a long time. In any event, we certainly support that principle.
Another measure I do not like in the Bill is a proposal to establish a citizens heritage fund. Even the Government of Alberta makes some wise proposals and points out that there will be competition for fund raising to get people to donate to this citizens heritage fund.
What is wrong with this idea? The Minister states that the money would not go toward usual activities and become a substitute for expenses that taxpayers would otherwise bear, but would be used for expansion purposes. Some environmental groups have been basically told that it is the only way our national parks will be expanded.
I point out, however, that any citizen who wants to make a donation to the Crown can do so through other current provisions. We do not need a special measure, and I believe some people would get upset, as people in the arts world were upset when there was a proposal that the National Gallery do
April 19, 1988

fund-raising in the private sector. All the small museums became worried that they would have trouble raising funds for their operations with such a big organization hustling funds from the same people.
Environmentalists should be concerned that this may happen with a citizens' heritage fund. We have a responsibility as citizens to have a public presence in the parks system. There should be no need for private fund raising in order to fulfil these obligations. Private citizens who have ample opportunity to make donations to smaller parks and other environmental causes should not be crowded out.
Further, the proposal would increase the leverage the Minister has over non-governmental organizations who would then have to apply for funding from this citizens' heritage fund. There is no proposal that it even be an arm's length agency, and this would be a very unhealthy development. I hope the Minister will reconsider that and drop this proposal. It has not been well accepted by the people most involved with national parks.
The Bill would permit certain subsistence activities. This is an important matter in the case of native people who have been using national park areas. As we hopefully expand the system in the future, this would be a very important measure. As well, non-native people in local areas have used parks for subsistence purposes. The idea is that they not be cut off from this source of livelihood. I would certainly agree with that, especially if this is a measure in the case of non native people, to include those people already involved but not necessarily to expand this practice.
It makes a great deal of sense in the case of native people in areas where we may want to see further park development and some kind of integrated way of carrying on traditional hunting and gathering activities. Native people are extremely good conservationists. This kind of combination of activity would be very desirable and suitable.
Another measure in this Bill about which we heartily approve is the increased penalties for poaching. I note that the Parliamentary Secretary spent a great deal of time talking about this section. I suppose this is the real motherhood section of the Bill. No one can object to it. We might even want some stronger measures. I understand the Government is going to entertain amendments for stronger measures in parts of the penalty section where the penalties are not quite strong enough for species of animals that are not rare. Everyone is on board in this one. This is something that environmentalists have been talking about for a long time. The penalties in place right now are, in effect, a licence to poach. They certainly do not discourage poaching. They do not adequately punish for such activities.
Members of the Liberal Party have spoken on this Bill. They have joined in condemning the Government for its inactivity with respect to national parks. I simply want to state that I
National Parks Act
think the Liberal Party does not have a leg to stand on. This is an area where the present Government has at least taken a few steps forward, although I do not think it has done enough in this area. We know of its record in slashing funds at the beginning of its mandate in the environmental area. We do not want to suggest that the Conservative Government is a model to follow. We would like things done very much differently. However, the Liberal criticism of the Conservative record is really far-fetched indeed.
There was a long, blank period on national parks under the Liberal Government when nothing was done. It was only because of considerable agitation from voluntary organizations and the non-governmental sector that we got some action. Of course, my Party was very active in fighting to get a national park on Ellesmere Island. Finally, we had a three-Party consensus and pressure was put on the Social Credit Government of British Columbia to get that deal negotiated, and we see the fruits of that consensus in Bill C-30 today. But it was tough going and we certainly did not see leadership from either the present Government or the previous Liberal Government with respect to those issues.
There are a number of housekeeping measures in Bill C-30. The present National Parks Act has been out of date for some time. We are in favour of good housekeeping. There are many minor measures that simply bring Bill C-30 up to date. However, some of these minor measures are perhaps not worded as carefully as they might be. We see the authorized use, regulated use-but how prudently regulated, we wonder- of pesticides and other toxic substances in the parks. I find even the contemplation of this a rather daunting prospect. There is certainly provision for spills in transportation. I suppose that has to be there if that kind of transportation is going to be permitted. But it is certainly a rather dismal prospect that there would be toxic substances used in the parks.
We have had pressure from the Government of Alberta and Conservatives from that province who would want to make greater use of pesticides, and who believe that we have to protect the human commercial areas adjacent to national parks. Not only do they want to encroach into the national parks but they want to reduce the naturalness of our national parks by allowing the use of these toxic substances, supposedly to protect commercial activities next to the parks. It is a very short-sighted approach, that profits in the short term are all we should be considering. We have thousands of toxic substances in use and we do not know what the impact will be on the environment. We would like to think there are some areas where there would be an absolutely total ban. I would like to think there are some areas where the use of chemical pesticides simply would not be contemplated.
National parks themselves would be threatened enough by the waters and by air coming into them from some other areas. The idea that we would permit or in any way encourage the use of chemical pesticides in national parks seems to me to be very unfortunate. Therefore, when we talk about regulation,

April 19, 1988
National Parks Act
does it mean zero regulation or some regulation? We have too many people in the pesticide business who think that as long as we do not have too much of it at any one time, it is all right. They completely forget the cumulative effect of chemical pesticides. The stuff does not go away. It is there in the soil, in the ground water and it continues to have its effect year after year after year.

Mr. Speaker, I will just take one minute to wrap up by saying that we certainly support this Bill. We think it is important. We want to see some further clarification and we are looking for certain amendments. I hope the Minister will address these questions very promptly. I hope this will be put into the context that we need stronger environmental protection. A Ministry which has slashed its budget in the environment, I think, has to answer these questions and not simply ask us to be confident that everything will be done properly. I think we need very precise assurances. Is the Minister going to give way on the ski areas? Is he going to give way on development? Is he going to put commercial interests ahead of conservation? I think he has to answer those questions. I hope he will answer them favourably.
We will support him in taking a very strong stand for the environment. This Bill goes some of the way but it does not go quite far enough. We would like to be very sure that mistakes are not made, that we get a very clear definition of wilderness areas so that we will have a National Parks Act of which we as Canadians can be proud, an Act which will ensure some protection for future generations.

Mr. Speaker, I was extremely surprised to hear the Hon. Member say that Liberal Governments did nothing for national parks. I know she has a reputation for telling the truth and I do not think that she would want to mislead the House. Any objective person who looks at our record will see that during the 1970s, the number of national parks was more than doubled. In fact, they were substantially
increased. I can recall when the Hon. Jean Chretien was appointed Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. At that time national parks was under that Ministry. The number of national parks in Canada was relatively small and were doubled, if not tripled. I can go through the list of national parks. I do not know the exact number but there was a substantial increase of national parks at that time. I was also the Minister responsible.
I challenge anyone in this House to look at the great increase in national parks under the Government of the Right Hon. Pierre Elliott Trudeau. There was a substantial increase not only in national parks but in historic places, in canals and waterways. There was a fantastic increase. I think to suggest otherwise to the House is simply to mislead the House and the country.
I might say as well that in the period when I was the Minister responsible for national parks, we did not always get the co-operation we wanted in establishing new parks from New Democratic and Conservative provincial Governments. As a matter of fact, very often they took a very dog in the manager approach to the creation of national parks in British Columbia, Manitoba, and Saskatchewan. I challenge anyone to look at the record and to stand by that kind of statement.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member talked only in generalities. He did not name one park. He did not name one square mile. He just talked about his wonderful record. I do not have the dates or the square miles with me either. I would be a little bit skeptical about these kinds of claims. Let him put on the record exactly what the Liberal achievement was. I do not think that it was very good. The result is that we have a relatively small part of our national heritage devoted to national parks after a very long period of Liberal Government. Let the Hon. Member be specific if he really wants to make that case.
I would be glad to.
I would be very glad to listen to him, but I am not impressed.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a couple of comments on the presentation of the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). I happen to enjoy one of the national parks in Saskatchewan. It is called Prince Albert National Park. Of course we go through the same kind of discussion there as to commercial activities versus environmental concerns.
The point I want to make is that we have to keep in mind that national parks are for people and, I suppose, for wildlife as well, but primarily for the enjoyment of people. I certainly want to protect these parks for centuries to come.
It seems to me that we tend to forget that we have to maintain a balance. I suggest that this is a rather imperfect
April 19, 1988

balance when we look at a figure of as little as 1 per cent or less. As a matter of fact, it would be a mere fraction of the total land surface of national parks devoted to some kind of town site with some commercial activity that is there to serve the needs of people. Of course, the thousands of square miles that are devoted to our heritage are there for conservation purposes.
I would like to ask the Hon. Member to expand a little and to try to demonstrate perhaps a little better understanding. In her presentation this morning I detected that she felt that the Act and that the Conservatives, particularly people from Alberta and western Canada, have no feeling for these concerns. I do not think that is accurate. I would like her to comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to comment on that very crucial question. The Hon. member talked about balance. My whole point is that the balance is too skewed the other way. If 98.5 per cent of land surface is devoted to commercial activity and 1.5 per cent is devoted to national parks, and then a lobby group of Alberta back-benchers is talking about reducing that 1.5 per cent to something smaller, then I think that the balance is entirely missing.
That is not true.

The Hon. Member said that I did not think people in the West or Alberta understood. My point is that there are many environmentalists, many people who are concerned to preserve some of our heritage, our physical heritage, for future generations. There are people who are concerned. I do not think that the Alberta Conservative caucus represents those people.
And you think you do?

Let me quote from one Alberta Member who said, "They could not offend anyone to do some angle drilling for gas and oil from outside the parks' boundaries". He does not see any objection to limited to moderate lumber developments. Good grief, this is just saying that we will use the national parks for making a fast buck, the same as the rest of the country. That is against the whole idea. Some areas need to be preserved as wilderness areas. Some areas must provide for the preservation of some species. There must be some areas where we human beings will not be boss and kill off everything else with chemical pesticides or what have you. There must be some areas about which we will be thinking for the future and where there will be some conservation.

Mr. Speaker, all I can say is thank goodness that the elks and the bears do not have television sets to watch and listen to this sort of nonsense. It is a prime example of a distortion of what in fact has happened. It makes me a little annoyed.
The point I am trying to make is that we have to strike a balance with respect to what the status quo is today, for
National Parks Act
example, when we take a look at a national park. I am all for including more national parks in the country. We have to take a look at setting aside town sites which represent probably less than 1 per cent of our national parks. Surely to goodness, as we do in our cities right now where we have such things as zoning by-laws, we have to be very careful as to what we will allow into parks. For goodness' sakes, let us separate the wilderness from the town sites. That is the point I am trying to make. I think that the Hon. Member has taken this to the extreme and has brought in all kinds of other issues which are totally unrelated.

Mr. Speaker, I think the problem is that some Conservative Members, and I believe it is true of some Liberal Members as well, want to have it both ways. They talk about wanting wilderness areas and everyone to be there to enjoy it. They must have restaurants and motels so that they can enjoy these wilderness areas in comfort. But then one cannot have a wilderness area if one has all these amenities. Let us not kid ourselves. That is ordinary tourism, which is perfectly desirable. I am not objecting to that. But there has to be something separate from that. There needs to be some areas which are wilderness areas that protect nature, that say this is an area in which the human destructive urges are going to be limited and we are going to keep something from being wrecked by the normal processes of civilization for the future.
You would think that the dinosaur club would like that.

Dinosaur club indeed. Let me quote another dinosaur who said that decisions regarding highway construction and maintenance should reflect the important role they play in Canada's economy and not be based solely on park land use criteria. This is saying that a park should not be a park, but a place where highways go and the normal economic criteria are the ones that would count. That is missing the whole point of having wilderness areas and having national parks.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to ask a question of the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald). A few moments ago the Hon. Member made reference to a particular Alberta Member of Parliament. I hope that she had a particular one in mind since I am going to ask her to identify that Member of Parliament. As I understood the Hon. Member, a particular Alberta Member of Parliament said or recommended that angle drilling and lumbering in national parks was all right. I would appreciate if the Hon. Member would identify the Alberta Member of Parliament and the source that she is using.
By making the statement as she did she brings into question all Alberta Members of Parliament and their positions on this issue.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome that intervention. I hope that the Hon. Member will rise and give a very strong

April 19, 1988
National Parks Act
pro-conservation, pro-environment, pro-parks speech. I think that would be very important.
I cannot give the Hon. Member the source of the quote right now. I will give it to him later. The Member I am quoting is the Eton. Member for Crow's Nest. With respect to the highway construction it is another one from the Alberta Government. I can give him the exact quote on the spot.
I am afraid that, again, we are dealing with NDP fear, fabrication and fantasy. In fact, there is no Member for Crow's Nest.

Mr. Speaker, first, I would ask the Hon. Member when she replies to my question to make any further comments.
We have been having an uproar in British Columbia because of the Government's attitude on Strathcona and the possible despoliation of Strathcona. I would like to ask the Hon. Member if she sees any possible replication in the Government's attitudes, the dinosaur club's attitudes in this Bill. Is there any potential replication of the Strathcona affair on Vancouver Island?

I apologize for the mistake. It was the riding of Crowfoot, and it is contained in a newspaper interview.
In answer to the Hon. Member for New Westminster- Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) I think the Strathcona situation in British Columbia is one of the most flagrant examples of the misuse of provincial parks. This is an example of simply rezoning an area that is supposed to be wilderness, or it had limited development, and calling it a recreational area, then mining, lumbering, and other economic activities can be allowed. I would hate to think that the Government would be so unenlightened, but the legislation is not clear enough. It does not state precisely what wilderness areas will be. It gives the Minister the right to designate wilderness areas, and it talks about activities consistent with protecting wilderness areas. Since there is little understanding about what a wilderness area is in the caucus at large, and I do not know if that is true for the Minister and I hope that he will clear it up, we must be a little worried. That could be dealt with by having a clear amendment about what is a wilderness area, in order that people will not have to be worried about a repeat of the Strathcona Park affair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. On debate, the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia).

Mr. Speaker, I know the Minister is anxious to close the debate. We are not only on the motion of the Minister, but on the motion of another Member whereby there could be further speakers. I think that it would add to the total quality of this debate if the Minister had an
opportunity to answer some of the questions asked and dispelled certain fears, some may be legitimate and some may not be, and concluded with the full knowledge of the criticism put forward rather than being attacked from the back, so to speak, after he has spoken.
I am glad to take the floor at this point. In answer to the question put forward by the Hon. Member for Edmonton South (Mr. Edwards), I would like to give him additional information now that he knows it is the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) who was quoted on angle drilling in parks as a possibility for exploitation. As to the source, we can only go by one that is highly reputable, because it comes from the city of the Hon. Member, and it is The Edmonton Journal for Tuesday, December 15, 1987.
Oh, oh!

Not only did it contain the gem of angle drilling, which everyone found quite amusing, but it also contained another interesting notion attributed to the same Hon. Member for Crowfoot, namely, the possibility that he sees room for some "limited to moderate lumber developments". That was contained in the same article.
Evidently we are dealing here with quotations. We all know from past experience that they are not all reliable. We will be glad to give the Hon. Member for Crowfoot the benefit of the doubt of a misquote.
Where we cannot give him or other colleagues from Alberta the same benefit of the doubt, because the source is solid and irrefutable, is in a letter from the Chairman of the Edmonton chapter of the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society dated January 10, 1988. In that letter, Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to your attention a couple of sentences in which Mr. Rasmussen writes: "I realize that the Alberta caucus is lobbying hard to alter or stall the Bill", namely Bill C-30. "Frankly, the Bill is not nearly strong enough in its protectionist stance. However, on behalf of the membership of my organization, I urge you", and this is a circular letter addressed to all Members of Parliament, "to move it in an unaltered form to a second reading in the very near future".
Mr. Rasmussen goes on to say, "The Alberta caucus is very much out of touch with Albertans on this issue". That is an interesting statement coming from someone in Edmonton, not from one of us here, or an unwashed Member of Parliament from Toronto. Mr. Rasmussen goes on to say: "The letters and editorials are unanimously against the development stance. In fact, there has not been a single letter", meaning letter to the editor, "supporting the stance of the Alberta caucus. The press in all other Alberta centres is running the same on this issue!"
The substance of this letter is that there is a national consensus to get this Bill going and through. The sentiments expressed by Mr. Rasmussen are such, coming from Alberta, that we have to take them into account and give them the credence and the weight that they deserve, unless Alberta
April 19, 1988

Members in the House would like to rise and debate the content of Mr. Rasmussen's letter dated January 10, 1988.
In detail the Bill contains a number of measures that we do support. Those measures are strangely reminiscent of a decision made in 1984 to amend the Bill. In other words, the Bill contains a set of measures, except for one or two, including the one that deals with the citizens' heritage fund, which have been available to the Government for action since it came into power in September, 1984, three and a half years ago.
As my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cochrane- Superior, did on Friday, we would like to express our support in general terms. On more than one occasion on Thursdays when the business of the House is called, the Liberal Party inquired with the House Leader of the Government as to when this Bill would be brought forward. That is something that does not happen very often.
Having analysed the Bill in depth, I have some reservations about the weakness of clauses 1.3 to 1.6 on pollution. It seems to me that those clauses need to be strengthened. Perhaps they were written in isolation from what we have been attempting to do on Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment. I would hope when the Minister will appear in committee he will find it possible to come forward with amendments that will strengthen the pollution clauses of the Bill. Perhaps today he has some comments to make to that effect.
In those particular clauses on the costs of clean-up, I would urge the Minister to review the Bill carefully as we are approving it on second reading. Since we will have an opportunity in committee to examine it clause by clause, I urge the Minister to come forward with an amendment to strengthen those clauses. If not, we in the Opposition will be prepared to do so, provided we receive the necessary support from Members on the government side.
The main controversy which has been raised by others is whether or not the Ministers can give us assurance, possibly today, on the question of boundaries in the ski area. That is definitely a source of great uncertainty, speculation, and unnecessary grief. In other words, we would like to be given the assurance that the Government will not come forward in committee with an amendment to the present Bill that will make the boundaries of Sunshine Village changeable by way of a cabinet decision. Therefore, the assurance today in the House that the boundaries of Sunshine Village will remain as they are proposed now at second reading would go a long way in removing fears on the part of all parties concerned, not only in the House, but those outside who follow the proceedings of this Bill very carefully.
I would love to engage, if time were to permit, but I will not, in putting on the record numerous national parks that were established in Liberal times just to straighten out the false
National Parks Act
impression which the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) has in relation to the Liberal record, which is a very fine and outstanding one. We are very glad to see that our record is being built upon at the present time in the life of this Parliament by Bill C-30, but there is no justification at all for the Member's statement made earlier.
The Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) indicated that the number of national parks introduced when he was the Minister runs into a dozen or more. It would take too much time to cite them all, but they stretch from east to west and from south to north. They are there to be seen by every Canadian who wants to enjoy the beauty and recreation that such parks offer. The national parks system is an outstanding one and it is the envy of every visitor from outside of Canada. What puzzles me is that the Government in October, 1986, in the Speech from the Throne announced the following:
Canada's national parks represent a heritage of great importance to the
present and future generations.
We agree. "My government" said the representative of the Queen in the Senate:
-will ask Parliament to approve major reforms to the National Parks Act.
Where are the major reforms in this Bill? They are extremely difficult to find. Maybe one could make the case for a major reform, as the Minister no doubt will try to do about the proposed citizens' heritage fund, but that is not something that can go by uncriticized because it has a number of flaws. In my view it is not in that category of initiatives. Why was it necessary for almost four years to go by to introduce a piece of legislation which so closely reminds us of decisions which were ready for this Government to make when it took power in September, 1984? That is a puzzle very few can answer.
The Government has demonstrated by this enormous delay since September, 1984,-when there was also a hiatus between two administrations and a lack of legislation-that it cannot manage in a competent manner the flow of legislative measures to be introduced in this House. This very measure we are debating here today, I submit, could have been debated in 1985, at the latest in 1986, because it was all there to be brought forward. No wonder if Canadians in communities across the country, who cherish and place a high value, understandably and quite rightly so, on our national parks systems and ways to strengthen and improve them, have become so frustrated. To add to that particular frustration is this uncertainty created in Alberta, in your own province, Mr. Speaker, as reflected in the letter written by Mr. Rasmussen which I read a few moments ago.
We have within the Alberta Progressive Conservative caucus two members, one is the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) whose tendency is to favour angle-drilling in national parks, and the other is the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), who would like, if one reads between the lines in what he said, our national parks to be turned into tourist playgrounds. That would be the ultimate joy and accomplishment

April 19, 1988
National Parks Act
for the Member from Bow River. On the one hand he finds that the taxation system on citizens of Banff and Jasper is too high, yet he had to admit that citizens do not want to switch to a municipal type of government as in any other part of the country. Evidently there are some advantages in the regime that Canadians in Banff and Jasper do enjoy, otherwise they would have already opted and decided in favour of introducing a municipal form of government in their own towns.
I would like to draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, the importance of spelling out the boundaries of the ski areas in the three parks, namely, Banff, Jasper and Riding Mountain, as this Bill does, and to obtain the assurance that these boundaries will remain entrenched in the Bill so that the assurance will be in a legislative form and changes will not be possible by way of an executive decision.
In moving on to the question of the citizens' heritage fund proposed by the Minister in Clause 8, the question is one that shifts the onus for the establishment of such a fund from the public to private initiative. The creation of a fund by way of a competitive effort with other efforts which take place every year and frequently in any community region and across the country is in itself a disadvantage. Second, the fund would be put at the disposal of the Minister and we would not know how that fund would be applied, how the decisions would be made on priorities, whether it would be a highly political fund or one whose utilization would be guided by principles having to do with the best interests of improving the quality and the extent of the national parks system. We do not think it will be a fund that will not be perceived as a slush fund by the public.
Therefore, we would much rather see an approach recommended by the task force on park establishment in November, 1986 of a 5 per cent minimum allocation yearly in Parks Canada's total annual budget to build up and develop over the next five years and more a capital acquisition fund. After a very few years that fund would be substantial, and it would allow acquisition with a degree of certainty. Money would be built up and everybody would know that by a certain date funds would be available. It would permit a gradual, constant, well planned expansion of the already fine system we have.
We are all trying to search for ways of establishing a capital acquisition fund for parks, and I do not want to knock down completely the proposal in Clause 8, but I can assure Hon. Members that it lends itself to a number of very legitimate criticisms which I am sure the Minister will take into account and deal with. I believe that out of general revenue which provides funds to the newly named Environment Canada Parks, the allocation ought to be established. Then there would be continuity and consistency so that in the long term these funds would be reliably built up.
When dealing with acquisitions of this size and with a program that is intergenerational, we want to provide for something that does not depend on the whims of economic
conditions as they exist from one year to the next or on the whims of the success or lack of success of fund-raising initiatives. This particular sector of public interest deserves stability and continuity of this nature.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), dealt on Friday with traditional subsistence activities and with Clause 4 in particular, and I would like to reinforce what he said. This is the measure that recognizes the fact that new national parks must not inhibit traditional activities carried on by local native people. We are glad to see that this measure is being introduced because it was part of a package that was ready for implementation in 1984. It commands the attention of all of us who are concerned about the stability of the economies of native people in national parks.
I will conclude by stressing the importance, as others have, of wilderness zones. If this Bill had been introduced in 1985, we would certainly be ahead with that particular activity. A policy was already in practice at that time. The removal of the powers of expropriation is a new feature which I do not support because I think those powers ought to be in the Bill. Expropriation ought to be used very carefully, of course, but there may be times, over a period of 20, 30 or 40 years, when we may want to use expropriation powers in a careful and thoughtful manner. Without those powers, our ability to establish new areas will be weakened.
I do welcome the poaching regulations contained in Clause 7, but I find that the fines for the poaching of game animals such as caribou, elk and deer are far too low. In light of a television program which appeared a couple of weeks ago, we see that poaching is now an activity which constitutes an emergency, and I hope that either today or in committee, the Minister will indicate that these fines will be strengthened in a manner that will make it prohibitive to conduct such activity. I thank you for your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, and I look forward to hearing the next Hon. Member,

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the support of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) on the need to have a clear definition of wilderness areas. I wonder if he could elaborate a bit on that. I wonder as well if he would comment on how much wilderness area we need.
Such a very small proportion of Canada is devoted to national parks. Would he therefore be in agreement that it would be desirable for Canada to have a much larger proportion of land devoted to national parks, particularly to wilderness areas within parks? Would he want to put a percentage figure on that?

Mr. Speaker, unlike the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), I do not have instant answers. On a matter of such complexity as wilderness zones, I do not know if anyone could give an immediate response by way of percentages or direct numbers.
April 19, 1988

Of course, there is an enormous potential for wilderness zones. One would want to put aside the largest possible acreage one could put his or her hands on in areas that would qualify and would be suitable. The concept is a very good one, and as I said in my intervention, this policy has already been in practice for some time.
The creation of a wilderness national parks status is something that we should examine in committee in great depth. Perhaps we could also find the correct phraseology to use in introducing such an amendment. We might even conclude, after studying the Bill, that there are certain parks, though perhaps not all of them, that could be set aside as wilderness reserves. Thus we could enhance and elevate the status of existing national parks. Obviously, in order to be successful with that, we would have to be very firm on pollution-control measures. As the Hon. Member knows, wilderness is easily affected by certain chemical products, and therefore we must establish the linkages necessary for the protection of wildlife over-all.

Mr. Speaker, because certain Hon. Members are not very familiar with the national parks system in Canada, and in particular the Hon. Member for Broadview- Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) who said that under Liberal Governments nothing had been done, is the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) aware of the fact that under the Trudeau Government alone, the following national parks were created: Kejimkujik in Nova Scotia, Kouchibouguac in New Brunswick, La Mauricie in Quebec, Pacific Rim in British Columbia, Forillon in Quebec, Gros Morne in Newfoundland, Pukaskwa in Ontario, Kluane in the Yukon Territories, Nahanni in the Northwest Territories, Auyuitiuq in the Northwest Territories, Grasslands in Saskatchewan, Mingan in Quebec and the Northern Yukon Park in the Yukon Territory which came at the end of the regime and was followed through by the Government opposite?
That makes 13 national parks created under the Trudeau Government alone, out of a total of 32. I said that they were doubled, but 1 was wrong. They were close to doubled since 13 out of 32 were created since 1968 when Mr. Trudeau came to power. That does not include the national historic sites of which there are now 80 in Canada, many of which were created under the previous Liberal Government, not to mention the heritage rivers and canals.
Is the Hon. Member also aware of the fact that in Canada we now have 180,000 square kilometres set aside for national parks, one of the largest areas in the world, and that most of those parks were created under Liberal Governments which were in power during that time and gave a high priority to national parks?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is highly qualified to ask this question because he is a former Minister concerned with northern affairs and national parks. He was
National Parks Act
personally involved in the establishment of some of the parks that he just mentioned.
As I said, the record speaks for itself, and it is an outstanding record. The system is there to be seen by visitors. I would not be surprised if the St. Lawrence Island National Park was also established by a former Liberal Government. I would not be surprised if Point Pelee National Park were in that category as well. I am not quite sure about Mount Revelstoke National Park and Elk Island National Park, but the fact is that the whole system was given momentum and great impetus by successive Liberal administrations. That does not mean that negotiations at times, as the Hon. Member indicated, cannot go on so long that sometimes a park is announced and launched when the Progressive Conservative Party is in power. The Bruce Peninsula negotiations started a long time ago, even before my time here. I would like to add to that Ellesmere, an area over which negotiations go back over a decade or so.
This is a very tricky field in which to claim paternity or maternity, but nevertheless the basic point is that the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood who unfortunately is not here to listen to us, made a statement that was a little bit off the mark, and that we in Canada have a fantastic network of parks of which we can collectively be very proud.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated.

Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me to participate in the debate today on Bill C-30. The Bill means a great deal to western Canada, if not to all of Canada.
First I would like to congratulate the Minister for introducing the Bill. It contains many excellent amendments to the Act and I want to commend him especially for the new poaching laws to protect wildlife. It is extremely important that our national parks be protected. The parks are there for everyone to enjoy, whether they be hikers, skiers, visitors, or even residents of one of the town sites such as Banff, Jasper, or indeed Waterton National Park.
Tourism and the environment can work together. We in the Conservative Party certainly do not want to promote a cement jungle or a Coney Island situation in any of our national parks. However, we feel that with open debate and meetings, with participation by the residents of the various parks, we can sit down and design a controlled-type of development that will be beneficial not only to those residents but to the provinces as well.
As you well know, Mr. Speaker, coming from that great province, we in Alberta have more square kilometres of national park than any other province and are very pleased and proud to have them. Within Banff and Jasper National Parks we have skiing facilities which have been in place for many years. I am a skier and have been for about 30 or 35 years. Since about 1965 or 1966 I spent almost every weekend during the ski season skiing at Sunshine, Lake Louise or even Marmot

April 19, 1988
National Parks Act
Basin up near your area. We are very proud of those skiing areas.
Our main problem today is that a lot of the facilities in those parks have to be replaced in order to make them competitive with other areas such as Whistler or indeed places like Aspen which have tremendous skiing facilities. I would like to see this Bill go to committee where the Minister can appear along with other witnesses to discuss how we can maintain some of these excellent skiing facilities in order to bring tourists and other visitors to our parks so they can enjoy the facilities.
Another area I wanted to discuss concerns the boundaries of the Towns of Banff and Jasper. It is noted in Bill C-30 that the Governor in Council may fix the boundaries of those two towns by an order adding a description of those boundaries as a schedule to the Act. I am very pleased to see that. The Minister has been very open and honest and feels he has to go to the residents of those areas and talk to them. He has to hear and see their concerns before carving the boundaries in stone. I must thank him for that move.
During the past two and a half years I have visited Jasper, Banff and Lake Louise and talked to their Chambers of Commerce as well as the residents about self-government. They also want self-sufficiency. They want to protect their areas. They do not want open development, they want controlled development so they can move towards selfsufficiency and reliability. I have to say that here again the Minister said he would have open meetings. He will listen to the people who live there, the people who are designing the future of those areas. Then, after close consultation with them and his officials, and indeed I hope the House, he will bring forward recommendations as to what the boundaries might be or indeed should be.
I think that is part of our efforts at national reconciliation, where the decisions are not made here in Ottawa without consultation. This Government is moving towards talking to the people in the provinces and the industry to decide what they need and what is best.
I have also had a lot of discussions with the Minister's department concerning land lease rates. The 1980 assessment value on properties in Banff, Jasper and Waterton National Parks proved to be perhaps too much of a hardship. Some of the rates increased by 2,000, 3,000 or 4,000 per cent. This Government does not feel that we should make a decision here and enforce it on people somewhere else in Canada, and we are reviewing the land lease rates and the assessment value of the various properties in those areas. A special committee has been formed which will make recommendations to the Minister. I know he will review those recommendations with all due care and try to make things more fair and equitable for the people who live in those areas.
With regard to the wilderness areas, it is very difficult to put boundaries on them. Perhaps many people here in the House
today have never visited some of these huge parks in western Canada. It would be totally impossible to lay out specifically all the boundaries for wilderness areas. The mountain ranges are very vast and the Minister would have a great deal of difficulty if he tried to carve those boundaries in stone.
I am very interested in Bill C-30. It should really go to committee where we can hear the concerns of the people from the various parks and also hear from representatives of the tourism industry why they want to maintain and upgrade their equipment in order to attract people to the parks.
Therefore, I would like to move:
That this House sit through the lunch hour for the purpose of continuing
consideration of Bill C-30, an Act to amend the National Parks Act and to
amend an Act to amend the National Parks Act.

Mr. Speaker, I feel decidedly of two minds about the continuation of the debate at the moment. It has been as badly handled as the parks system of Canada very often has been. This debate began Friday when the Minister was not here and other people, including our critic on the environment, were not here to take part in the debate. The debate blundered on this morning with one of the Members from Alberta speaking first.
The Minister has been sitting there quietly not saying a word. He has had several opportunities to speak to the matter. He is, I am sure, taking it all in, but we expect the Minister to make a statement on the Bill, to make a defence of it. Rather, he sits there quietly, wanders around behind the curtains, and pays some attention to the debate. When does he intend to get into it and give us a defence of what he has put forward? More significantly, when does he plan to deal with those shortcomings in the Bill which have not been provided for?
There has been a nice debate between members of the Official Opposition and the Government on who should get credit for the development of the parks system. Longevity always helps in these matters and the Liberals, having had the privilege of governing this country for so much of this century, can, of course, take credit for a good deal of parks creation. However, to ensure that the parks system is maintained and provided for through legislation is surely the responsibility of the present Minister.
The Bill has significant shortcomings. It fails in a number of very important areas to provide for what is already supposedly the policy of the Government. For a private Member of the governing caucus to pull this particular stunt, with the
April 19, 1988

connivance of the Ministry of course, while the Minister sits there quietly not having said anything in the debate so far, seems to me to be a contemptible use of this House by the Conservative Government.
It is truly contemptible to interfere with the proper order of the day, to attempt to conclude the matter today by speaking through the noon hour when the debate on something which is of enormous importance to Canadians has barely started. The Government House Leader smiles his sarcastic smile and serves up another piece of the arrogance of the Conservatives which we have seen all too often.
With those comments on the way in which this has been done, let me turn to Bill C-30, which is of such enormous importance to all Canadians who recognize the need for a well developed parks system. Canadians recognize that Canada, which covers such a large part of the earth's surface, has responsibility for its large natural resources and has all too often been preoccupied with the economic value of those resources. Canadians recognize the importance of the parks system in ensuring that some small part of Canada's territory will be set aside in preserves, in parks, to be enjoyed for decades and centuries to come in as close as possible to its pristine state.
I had intended to ask the Member who has just pulled this parliamentary trick on us whether she is in agreement with the Minister of Forestry, Lands and Wildlife in the Alberta Government who has suggested that we need more ski hills in the parks. A good part of the Member's quite short speech was a celebration of skiing in the mountains of Alberta and British Columbia. That certainly leaves me suspicious that she is not all that committed to the development and maintenance of our parks system.
The way in which this whole matter has been treated leaves me acutely suspicious, together with my colleagues in the New Democratic caucus, that the Conservatives have gone some distance toward doing what they had to do, that is, providing legislative amendments which the operation of the parks and the working responsibility of the officials absolutely required. However, they have neglected to put into this Bill those matters which have apparently already been established as government policy.
Given this particular manoeuver, I find it more difficult to say that we in our caucus are supportive of Bill C-30 as far as it goes. This Bill dates back to 1930 and was only amended significantly once, in 1974. As our sensitivity to the needs of the parks has developed and as the threat to the parks system has become more acute, there has been a very significant advance in our understanding of what is required. The failure of the Government to provide for that in this Bill leaves us with constrained support. To provide legislative housekeeping needed for the smooth operation of the national parks is a basic necessity for good administration. To put current parks policy into legislation is again taking a very small step.
National Parks Act
The Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), who does like to celebrate his own accomplishments and to put on a fine front before the environmentalists of the country, could do a lot better than he has in this Bill. He could have done a lot better by speaking to the Bill and possibly opening himself up to some questions and comments, although the rules of the House tend to constrain that in ways which are quite detrimental.
I find it particularly unfortunate that it seems to be the intention to have the entire second reading debate in as brief a time as possible. It was thrown into the House on Friday and they want to wrap it up on the following Tuesday and get it into legislative committee. Lord knows what sort of attacks on the parliamentary process will take place in the committee.
My friend, the Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald), has already pointed out the need for far more frankness by the Government in dealing with the parks system of the country. That was a point made in a briefing note to my colleagues and myself.
The refusal of the Minister to rise to the occasion and speak on policy and his refusal to come to grips with the needs of the parks system and to ensure they are met, only underscores the Government's lack of frankness.
This country needs a government that will support parks as natural preserves, not as tourist sites to attract floods of people. Obviously, we want Canadians to have an opportunity to appreciate and enjoy natural preserves, but that calls for careful control of how we operate them. We want to ensure that the Government is committed to that kind of principle.
We need a government that will allocate resources to parks development with the funds of Canadians, without opening the kinds of possibilities that obtain with the citizens, heritage fund proposal of the Minister. There must be a clear commitment by the Government through taxpayers' funds to ensure that the parks system is maintained and expanded. Obviously this means that there must be clear evidence that the Government is really committed without equivocation to the development of the national parks system of Canada. There are very serious questions about whether that is really the case.
For example, the concept of wilderness is integral to the concern about natural preserves. Only when we know how those within the Government responsible for the parks system envisage wilderness will we be assured that the preserves will remain in perpetuity for the people of Canada to enjoy. The Bill does not provide for that because there is no definition. One is left guessing at the Government's intention as to what wilderness may be.
The fact that the suggestion for activities within these parks include aircraft and surface transportation rates is a real concern. We are particularly suspicious of Conservative caucus members from Alberta who want highways development in

April 19, 1988
National Parks Act
parks removed from the control of the department responsible for the parks. There is a very clear danger that in spite of our desire to maintain wilderness areas, roads will be built to cut through these parks and thereby violate the sense of wilderness and the entire ecology of the park system. The failure to define wilderness in the Bill leaves us with no assurance that this fundamental need within the parks system will be met by the Government.
Another concern is the lack of clear provision for certain subsistence activities that can be carried on in parks. This is a concern that arises as parks are established in northern areas and places where aboriginal peoples still subsist on the natural resources and wildlife. We must take into account the treaty rights and more recent land negotiation agreements with our aboriginal peoples when we are establishing these parks. We want to ensure that in allowing these activities to continue in some parks there is a clear definition of them within the legislation. The failure to do so properly in Bill C-30 arouses a great deal of concern.
We must be concerned that others may try to assume the rights being given to aboriginal peoples, which represents more than just the thin edge of the wedge. As the wedge opens the park more and more to these activities what assurances are there that the desire to maintain the preserves as much as possible will be respected in these circumstances?
The Government's failure to define these matters clearly are reasons for the constrained support and concern about the Minister's and the Government's policy on parks that I have been expressing.
These concerns find their greatest expression in two of our greatest and oldest national parks in the Rockies, in which the towns of Jasper and Banff are located. There has been a certain amount of skiing activity in these parks for some time. The Bill does not provide us with proper assurance with respect to the boundaries of the town sites within the parks, and that substantial commercial development along with ski development will be carefully controlled within the parks.
I wish to pursue some even greater concerns than those particular elements in the Bill I have discussed. There is the matter of the establishment of national marine parks. If anyone listening thinks that these remarks have been rhetoric brought up for the occasion, particularly as we speak into the lunch hour, let me say clearly and firmly that in the matter of national marine parks it is anything but rhetoric. Here we see one of the most significant indications of the failure of the Minister, which makes it no surprise to me that he sits there silent, ashamed to get up and speak to the Bill.
We have the opportunity to establish parks along shorelines in various places to add significantly to what already exists within our large land-based parks in the nation. The Government has declared its policy that there will be marine parks, but in this grab bag of amendments to the National Parks Act there is no clear provision for the establishment of these marine parks.
That is particularly unfortunate given the fact that the existing Act, in another of its shortcomings, does not provide clearly for the process by which territory is acquired. The Government of Canada gets the rights to territory and gradually works through the process of creating a national park. That process is not provided for in the existing National Parks Act, so difficulties arise. The Government of Canada has to use one Act and another Act, one form of authorization and another form of authorization, in dealing with provincial Governments, which generally have the rights of the Crown in ownership, if you will, of natural resources. In dealings with provincial Governments, the federal Government has great difficulties in carrying the process through.
The Minister walks out of the House, presumably off to his lunch, leaving behind a Bill which has not provided properly for a process for the acquisition of territory and the process of establishing a park. That seems to me a monstrous shortcoming in the Bill. He should have a declaration of policy for the establishment of national marine parks when the process is finally concluded, a process which has, by ministerial directive and under one pretext or another, to be carried forward. Not to have the final basis provided for the final destination of the process, if you will, and a national marine park provided, only underscores how limited Bill C-30 really is.
As a Member of Parliament from Northern Ontario, whose riding includes a vast chunk of northwestern Ontario land, small lakes, rivers and so on, my constituency has Lake Superior located on its southern border. Lake Superior is a great body of water. As we all know it is the largest lake of this kind on the face of the earth. It has one national park, a territory abutting on the north, but no necessity in our concern to provide natural preserves for the establishment of a marine park on Lake Superior.
I am not the only one who feels that lack. I am particularly critical of the failure to provide for national marine parks. We should have a basis for establishing such a park on Lake Superior, to draw this great lake to the attention of Canadians from coast to coast, and people from other countries as well, and encourage them to enjoy a part of it. It should be something as close to the pristine state as we can find.
