subsubtopic: RESOLUTIONS ON JOB EQUALITY FOR WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Party of Canada held its convention over the week-end and, on that occasion, several resolutions of great importance if women are to achieve social equality were passed because the Liberal Party is convinced that women must get the help they need to achieve equality in society. This means that work in the home must be considered as the responsibility of both parents and of society as a whole. This means that education and training circles must be made aware of the special needs of women. Job equality and equal pay for equal work programs must be carried out immediately and remain in force as long as women's wages are not equal to men's.

responsibilities who want to have some time to spend with their children.

subtopic: OBJECTION TO VARIETY STORE SERVICE IN HAMILTON
OBJECTION TO VARIETY STORE SERVICE IN HAMILTON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to report on a meeting that I attended Sunday evening with two dozen very concerned residents in a fashionable new housing development on the Mountain in my riding.
The problem that my constituents raised with the Minister responsible for Canada Post is this. With no door-to-door mail delivery anywhere in the area there is only one tiny postal counter, and it is located in a variety store which is right next door to a strip joint: "Girls, Girls, Girls, Six Nights a Week", and a hard rock club, all of which suggests that this convenience store provides considerably more variety than usual.
My neighbours told me bluntly that what we do not need is our wives and children being molested because of a strip joint next door to a so-called convenience store.
I toured the area and was appalled at the proximity of a rack of pornographic magazines and tapes no more than six feet away from the postal counter. Surely this shabby situation is unacceptable.
I urge the Minister and Canada Post to take immediate action to provide this new, large and growing community with proper mail service, and preferably door-to-door delivery.

subtopic: GINN CANADA TAKEOVER-CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
GINN CANADA TAKEOVER-CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government's approval of the sale of New American Library to Penguin Books appears to have given the final death blow to the Baie Comeau book publishing policy. Over and over again the Government has stated that it is committed to building a Canadian publishing industry, but recent government actions demonstrate otherwise.
The 1985 Baie Comeau book publishing policy stipulated that in any takeover of a Canadian based publishing company or subsidiary, either directly or indirectly through an international merger, a foreign buyer must find a majority Canadian partner for the subsidiary within two years.
Last month the Government announced its offer to buy 51 per cent equity control of Ginn Canada from American entertainment conglomerate Gulf and Western. However, it appears to have allowed the retention of a veto power over significant operating decisions. This offer does not make good business sense for Canadian management, because it disallows and disavows Canadian control.
Now, with the NAL takeover, the Government has shown a total lack of commitment not only to its own policy but to the building of a Canadian publishing industry. It is time that the Government re-read Baie Comeau, this time the lines, not just between them.

SOCIAL POLICIES OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY

Mr. Speaker,

Can the Prime Minister tell us if these representatives of the federal Government, these high public servants, are indeed authorized to negotiate something in terms of monetary settlement or support? Are they talking specifically about a deal? Are they talking specifically about offering human resources, technical resources in translation? Are they indeed talking to the Government of Saskatchewan about the constitutional rights that exist in Saskatchewan today in terms of education?

Mr. Speaker, indeed I have stated in Saskatchewan that which I have stated here and elsewhere. In my judgment, and I believe in the view of my hon. friend, minority rights are indivisible. You either believe in the protection of minority rights or you do not. You do not believe in them three-quarters of the time or half the time. That is the position that I adopted in Saskatchewan and it is the same position in Manitoba, Quebec, or British Columbia.
When minority constitutional rights could have been constitutionalized in 1982, because that is the only way in which to protect them fully, I think it was a source of regret to everyone that that was not done. I think that is a source of deep regret not only to my hon. friend but to many of us.

April 19, 1988
Presence in the Gallery
Linguistic minorities were left hanging out in 1982. Moreover, what is a matter of deep concern to me is that at that time provincial Premiers were given the right of constitutional over-ride in certain provisions. In exchange for what? This remains to be seen.
That is the constitutional position I have taken. I deeply deplore, as do the people in Saskatchewan, that there were not better protections at that time. L'Association des fransaskois is concerned as well with the residual implications of the Supreme Court decision, as am I.
With regard to the future, Premier Devine has set out his wish that Saskatchewan become bilingual. I think it is an important step forward for Canada that a Premier of a western province make that statement. As Prime Minister of Canada, I have genuinely encouraged Premier Devine along that road. 1 think it would be an important new advance for Canada in this regard. To that extent representatives of the Government of Canada are there working with the representatives of the Government of Saskatchewan to bring what I hope will be a greater degree of fairness to the province, a greater degree of understanding of this sensitive matter, and a greater degree of support for the French language minority in the Province of Saskatchewan, to enable them to preserve their language, their heritage, and their contribution to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. As the Hon. Member knows, if people arrive in Canada without proper documentation there is a process to be followed in terms of immigration officials. As long as we are aware that people will show up for their immigration hearing, we do not like to detain them. We are not in the business of detaining people. As soon as we receive that assurance, we do not detain them any longer. That is why we need the two immigration Bills C-84 and C-55 in order that we can turn around as soon as possible refugee claimants who are not genuine.
The immigration officials deal with each of those cases on an individual basis when they first arrive in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two of the Guatemalan leaders in exile who returned to Guatemala on April 18 were arrested as they deplaned. They have since been released, which we welcome, and think that it will encourage further moderation and dialogue in Guatemala.
Our Ambassador to Guatemala has expressed to the President the concern of Canadians with respect to the safety and well-being of those individuals. We will continue to make representations in that respect.

The House proceeded to the consideration of of Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and of human life and health, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have several observations with respect to the matter that is in front of the House at the present time.

There are 31 motions in amendment for consideration at the report stage of Bill C-74, an Act respecting the protection of the environment and human life and health. After much deliberation and especially discussion with the concerned Members, I am now ready to make a ruling on the grouping and voting pattern for the report stage.

Motions Nos. 1, 5(a) and 31 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) cause the Chair some procedural difficulty. I will deal with parts (b) and (c) of motion No. 5 later. These three motions in amendment refer to aboriginal peoples. The Hon. Member is attempting to introduce into Bill C-74 a definition of aboriginal peoples which is designated in section 35 of the Constitution Act. Unfortunately, by inserting this particular definition, the Hon. Member is increasing the scope of the Bill to a stage beyond what was agreed to at second reading. The only
reference already included in the Bill is to reserves or surrendered lands subject to the Indian Act which, of course, concerns Indians or Metis but not specifically Cree or Naskapi bands. Therefore, I am of the opinion that to include this particular definition of "Aboriginal Peoples" takes the Bill beyond what was originally envisaged, consequently I must rule these amendments out of order. Therefore, motions Nos. 1, 5(a) and 31 will not be put to the House.
Motion No. 2 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) was moved in the committee during its study of the Bill. The legislative committee had debated at length similar amendments which were negatived on recorded divisions. Nevertheless, after consultation with the Hon. Member, he has made the case that this matter of "establishing national standards" is of such significance that it warrants further consideration as permitted under Standing Order 114(10). Accordingly, Motion No. 2 will be debated and voted upon separately.
Motions Nos. 3, 5(b), 5(c), 7, 20, and 21 standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) are also a cause of some procedural difficulty to the Chair. Each of these motions in amendment attempts to insert into the Bill additional aspects based upon the James Bay and Northern Quebec agreement. These further motions go beyond the scope of the clauses which they attempt to amend. However important and worthy these proposed changes may be, I feel that I must declare them procedurally unacceptable in accordance with Beauchesne's Fifth edition at Citation 773(1). Consequently, they will not be put to the House.

Motion No. 2
That Bill C-74 be amended in Clause 2 by striking out lines 19 and 20 at
page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
(f) endeavour to establish national standards of environmental quality.
He said: Madam Speaker, I want to thank you for the acceptance of this motion which is extremely important. It deals with a question that strikes at the very heart of the Bill itself having to do with the importance of recognizing the establishment of national standards of environmental quality.
The Bill as worded now is weak and reveals on the part of the Government a lack of political will in acting as it speaks. The Government announced that this Bill is the greatest measure to clean up the environment, which it does not, and will open up a new era for the protection of the environment from damage that could be caused by new products, which it does attempt to do. But in endeavouring to do that the Government shies away, it withdraws and is afraid to put forward and entrench in the Bill, which is to be known as the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, the notion that it will establish national standards of environmental quality for the protection of Canadians.
It is interesting to note, and I want to bring it to your attention as forcefully as I can, Madam Speaker, that when this Bill was the object of public consultations in draft form it had in it exactly what I am proposing this afternoon. I draw your attention to page one of the draft Bill entitled Proposed Environmental Protection Act. On page one you will find in subparagraph (b) the following:
provide leadership in the establishment of nationally consistent standards of
environmental quality,
I repeat, "standards of environmental quality". That phrase has disappeared and one wonders why because it was a good
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
phrase. It received substantial and widespread support throughout the country in the process of public consultation, but it has gone. This is why at committee it became absolutely essential to put forward again this phrase, this concept, that in the duties of the Government in applying this Bill national standards of environmental quality be established. Instead what we have here, and what we object to, is this phrase which simply says "endeavour to establish nationally consistent levels of environmental quality". This is a far cry, quite different and extremely weak in comparison to the wording, "establish national standards of environmental quality".
The way the Bill is drafted now puts the emphasis on consistency. The way that Motion No.2 as proposed by us reads is to establish national standards. The difference that I want to bring out as clearly as I can is between the public relations effort of the Government in appearing to be the defender of environmental quality and the substance it delivered.
There was the impression, as I read from page 1, subparagraph (b), that the Government would provide leadership in the establishment of nationally consistent standards of environmental quality, but when it comes to the crunch the Government retreats into the words, "nationally consistent levels of environmental quality". What a sham, Madam Speaker. No wonder Canadians are catching up with the Government because they are beginning to see through the smokescreen which the Government has attempted to create not only with environmental matters. Here is a glowing and classical example of abandonment of the Government's stand when it launched the Bill and the substance we are facing today at report stage debate. This is why we objected in committee.
I am glad and very grateful to the Chair for having overruled the Chairman of the committee who ruled out of order what is now Motion No. 2 when we were in committee. I am extremely grateful because Mr. Speaker understood the importance of this amendment, its validity and its acceptability as we now have an opportunity to debate it in the light of the ruling a few minutes ago.
I cannot stress sufficiently and with enough vigour and passion the importance of this clause covered in Motion No. 2. When a government retreats from the policy concept of establishing national standards into the comfortable mushy world of endeavouring to establish nationally consistent levels, the Government does a 180 turnaround and says "Look, what we are really going to achieve is the lowest common denominator, that is what we will accept". The lowest, weakest standard that will be established in one part of the country will become our guiding principle in the application of our duties in relation to this particular legislation. There will no longer be national standards but only consistency. There will no longer be the strongest possible standards from the point of view of the public interest. We will only use what the weakest element in the link will be willing to accept. I do not want to mention any

April 19, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
region or any particular province because that would be unfair and premature.
I draw your attention, Madam Speaker, to the serious implication of the departure in political and policy terms that this Government has made by abandoning the concept that existed in the draft legislation and what came out of the committee as a result of the clause-by-clause analysis. I see you are indicating that my time is up, Madam Speaker. I will sit down, but again I want to express my gratitude to the Chair for having overruled the decision, thus permitting the debate on this particular amendment to occur today.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we are very pleased that this Bill has now proceeded to report stage on the floor of the House of Commons. We spent many weeks on it in committee. We debated a number of amendments that were put to the committee, and of all the committees on which I have worked, it seems to me that there was the greatest amount of co-operation extended on the legislative committee on this Bill under the direction of Barry Turner, the chairman at the time, and I know you are telling me that I should not be mentioning any names, Madam Speaker, but I have forgotten his riding, one of those great Ottawa ridings.
A number of witnesses appeared before the committee. A number of amendments were debated, the vast majority of which were passed. The members of the committee had the sense that we wanted this to be the finest environment Bill that had ever come to the House of Commons because this is the first environment Bill that has come to the House of Commons for 11 years. The amendment before us indeed was debated at great length in the committee. The amendment deals with national standards as opposed to nationally consistent levels.
For the first time, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act will provide an ecosystem management approach to environmental protection, an approach that protects the Canadian environment against the contamination of our air, our waterways, our soils and the marine environment. For the first time, we will have an Act with real teeth.
Clause 33 of the Canadian Environmental Protection Bill gives the Government broad powers to regulate against substances that harm the health and/or the environment of Canada and its citizens. These regulations will define national standards of control on the toxic substances now threatening our nation.
The Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), who has just spoken, proposed a seemingly minor amendment to the administrative duties section of the Bill. He has recommended that we make one word change by substituting the word "levels" for the word "standards" so that subclause 2(f) would require the Government of Canada to endeavour to establish nationally consistent standards, not levels, of environmental quality.
Although I recognize the Hon. Member's intention is to further strengthen this important piece of legislation, to adopt his seemingly innocent word change would be to impair the very goal he seeks. Consider the fact that subclause 2(0 lies within the administrative duties part of the Bill, the part that establishes the framework for the functioning of the Bill. It establishes a framework of flexibility, reflecting the very complexity of environmental management in a country this size and in this day and age.
The establishment of environmental standards, as requested by the Hon. Member, is an option under the Bill's regulatory apparatus. The replacement of the word "levels" with the word "standards" under the administrative duties part of the Bill would limit its regulatory powers to but one regulatory option which would be that of standards.
The Canadian Environmental Protection Bill, by signalling the Government's intention to establish nationally consistent levels, not standards, of environmental quality, is also signalling its refusal to limit itself to just one option of environmental control. The word "levels" allows for a range of regulatory possibilities, guidelines for industries to follow, objectives to be aimed at, codes of practice to be adhered to, standards to be achieved and outright bans to be implemented if required.
Canada's acid rain program is a case in point. The federal Government did not establish standards that would have prescribed emission limits at specific sources. Rather, it established an objective, the famous 20 kilograms of sulphur dioxide per hectare per year, as necessary for the protection of the Canadian environment. The provinces east of Saskatchewan have agreed to that objective and each of them is working to control its emissions to help meet that objective.
Flexibility of action is the key here. The provinces have different industries with different technologies. How they meet that objective is left to them. To call for national standards of environmental quality is to restrict unduly the many options for environmental control and to impair the capacity of the Government to offer Canadians the environmental protection they are demanding. I would ask that Hon. Members reject the proposed amendment to subclause 2(f).

Madam Speaker, I rise to support the amendment proposed by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), and I would like to thank the Chair for allowing this debate on such an important matter by in effect overruling the decision of the committee which tried to dispose of it by simply denying the importance of this question. We will now have a debate in the House on this absolutely crucial, vital matter.
Subclause 2(f) of the Bill simply says that we endeavour to establish nationally consistent levels of environmental quality. That is the obligation set out in the Bill, but the obligation is to establish nationally consistent levels, and the clause only requires that we endeavour to do so. How weak can the wording be? The amendment merely asks that we endeavour
April 19, 1988

to establish national standards of environmental equality. I believe the wording ought to be far, far stronger than that.
The Brundtland Commission report entitled Our Common Future, The World Commission on Environment and Development, concluded the following:
-national governments should establish clear environmental goals and enforce environmental laws, regulations, incentives and standards on industrial enterprises.
This should normally be done at the national level with local governments being empowered to exceed, but not to lower, national norms.
This is a proposal of the UN World Commission headed by the Prime Minister of Norway. The report has been approved in principle by the federal and provincial Governments. They say in principle we want this excellent protection for the environment, but here we have a specific piece of legislation and they do not stand up to be counted. They are not there when it comes to actually having national standards. Guidelines are weaker.
The committee heard in detail from environmental groups coast to coast, national, provincial and local groups, all kinds of experts and concerned citizens, about environmental protection and the need for really strong national standards. Let me just quote some of the advice given to the committee, now to the House, and so far ignored by the Government. Pollution Probe is a major environmental group and I quote them:
In Clause 8, CEPA leaves out one of the strongest tools that can be used for environmental protection-legally enforceable standards. Not all numbers related to environmental protection need to be standards, but not to have the option of using them is simply short-sighted, and limits available tools for use in the future.
I could not agree more. Let me quote Friends of the Earth:
The Bill should provide the opportunity to set numeric standards for ambient environmental quality, discharge limitations, or any other area which can be appropriately regulated in this manner and delete the reference to guidelines since they would allow for displacement of truly enforceable regulatory tools.
It is perfectly clear what the advice is but, I am sorry to say, it is being ignored by the Government. Let me quote the Environmental Law Centre, a major source of expertise on the subject:
It is unfortunate that the guidelines to be formulated by the Minister will not be legally binding. They should be given legislative force and enacted as regulations. The Minister should be given authority to issue standards.
The language is perfectly clear. Toxic Watch Project said this:
The absence of the word "standards" from this clause is a concern especially since CEPA repeals the Clean Air Act. The federal government must be able to set standards since only standards can be enforced.
To quote that group further:
The federal government should have the ability to set national minimum standards with provincial authority to exceed such standards.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
I heartily agree that the provinces should have the opportunity to set higher standards where they believe they are necessary for conditions in their own provinces. However, we should have nothing but the best national standards to ensure there will not be pollution ghettos and that some province will opt out or there will be negotiations whereby some kind of agreed upon objective is accepted as the only one politically saleables. In short, one that is not good enough.
Let me quote the Canadian Labour Congress, which participated in these hearings:
The federal government should have authority to establish strong minimum
national standards.
Let me be clear that this kind of advice came from all across the country. No province with environmental groups said anything different. All across the country there is agreement that environmental questions require minimum national standards. Why? Because environmentalists understand that pollution does not stop at provincial or municipal boundaries. Rivers cross international and provincial boundaries. Underground water crosses all kinds of boundaries. This very parochial approach does not take into account the reality that all life is connected, that pollution travels by air and by water, and that it is extremely important to have thoroughly adequate national standards.
Some of us thought we were going to get them. We thought we were going to get something at least close. The Minister stated earlier that there would be consultation with the provinces. He said that under the new amendment the federal Government is not compelled to consult with the provinces before taking action in cases where it is going to be necessary to act without it. Instead, where a province can convince the federal Government that its regulations are as strong or stronger than federal regulations and that the province is actively enforcing them, both Governments can enter into an agreement that ensures the requirements of the federal legislation are met.
The idea was that the federal Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) would publish a report on the status of agreements worked out with the provinces and they would be made public so people would be able to look at the adequacy of the agreements. Further, any group of 12 provincial residents can petition the federal Minister if they believe the province is failing to honour the agreement. In that case the federal Minister would be required to investigate and respond within 90 days. The Minister said the effect of the relevant provisions would be to create a mechanism for provincial accountability for the environment through federal statute. In his view those provisions, along with others in the Act, have the potential to create an unprecedented level of integration and co-operation between the federal and provincial Governments on environmental issues in a way which respects the jurisdiction of both.
That is what the Minister said. Subsequently he introduced new amendments that went against it. We saw the Bill being weakened. I think it is extremely unfortunate that the very

April 19, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
high standards Canadians wanted are not going to be achieved at ail in this Bill. We hope there will be some modest effort toward reducing pollution in the future but we should not have any illusions at all that this Bill will achieve any kind of cleanup whatsoever.
Therefore, I very much support the wording proposed by the Hon. Member for Davenport. It is modest but it is certainly in the spirit of the Brundtland Commission report. It is strongly supported by environmental groups across the country and would indeed make the Act stronger and contribute to giving Canadians the kind of protection they want for the environment. I strongly urge all Hon. Members to accept this amendment because we will end up with a far better Bill.

Madam Speaker, I was very impressed with the amendment presented by my colleague from Davenport. He may well be referred to as the Hon. Member from Italy or Zimbabwe or the European National Council because he is internationally renowned in the field of environmental studies, environment control, and certainly very knowledgeable in the field of pollution. If he felt there was an error in the way the Government structured the wording of this Bill, I suggest that we pay close attention to what he has to say.
Obviously this Bill will be touted by the Government as a great piece of pollution control. It will be a feather in the cap of the Government, a centre-piece of the Government's approach on the election trail. Yet it really is a bunch of smoke and mirrors that does not clean up the environment and control pollution. Let us not have any illusions. If the Government is serious about going through with a very important piece of legislation, let it be open enough to acknowledge the fact that we have to strengthen it. That, it seems to me, is not such a terrible thing. I think it would be in the Government's best interests.
The Parliamentary Secretary said it is just a minor word we are talking about, that all the Hon. Member wants to do is change the word "levels" to "standards", and I think that speaks reams.
I would suggest that the Meech Lake virus is creeping in here. The Member knows that within the Meech Lake concept one must establish national standards in order for the provincial governments to co-operate with the federal Government. That is exactly what they are trying to avoid doing by establishing the proper wording which has been recommended by my colleague, that is:
That Bill C-74 be amended in Clause 2 by striking out lines 19 and 20 at
page 2 and substituting the following therefor:
"(0 endeavour to establish national standards of environmental quality;"
-instead of leaving it as it presently is under "Administrative Duties", "Duties of the Government of Canada":
(f) endeavour to establish nationally consistent levels of environmental
quality;"
You and I, Madam Speaker, know very well that we have had enough examples of the establishment of low quality criteria in some provinces while other provinces have been very concerned and very effective. To include this clause puts the lowest common denominator in place rather than the approach which my colleague has suggested which has been supported by the Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald).
We are asking the Government to adopt this seemingly innocent change which has a powerful impact and is worth serious consideration rather than the light approach taken by the Member of the Government. This is an enforceable tool which makes it worth while. I am very glad that the Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) brought this forward so that we can address it.
The Brundtland Commission said that we should establish and enforce national standards on enterprises. We need this excellent protection. As the Member for Broadview- Greenwood pointed out, pollution does not recognize boundaries whether international, national, provincial, or municipal. If this will enable us to effect that kind of change the Government should gladly accept it and be appreciative of what the Member for Davenport has done.
I want to conclude by quoting something said by Mr. Higgins, a senior Canadian Government official, before the committee. He said:
The term "standard" in the context of environmental quality standard is one that has had some considerable debate within the environmental regulatory community in Canada. In terms of developing water quality guidelines, the Canadian Council of Resource and Environment Ministers attempted to define various terms to allow for a differentiation of them. Perhaps I could read what they have described as a water quality standard:
"It is an objective that is recognized in enforceable environmental control laws of a level of government.
I think that is what the committee is suggesting-that members of the committee would like to see, within this particular section of the legislation, the ability of the Minister to set such standards, which would be enforceable in law.
That is what is wrong with many of the Bills the Government has brought in. They all say certain things in essence but have no teeth which enable us to move forward in a concrete way in order to realize the goals which are enunciated but not carried out in the legislation. This is a perfect example of such misuse of words and intent. I hope that the House will support the motion put forward by the Hon. Member.

Madam
Speaker, I want to participate briefly in the grouping of motions before us. I am particularly interested in the clause which relates to legally enforceable standards. It is important that we place in law the strength necessary to provide rules that make clear what is required. Not all aspects of environmental protection need to be chiselled in stone, but we must be able to examine them and adhere to them.
In Clause 8, for example, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act leaves out one of the strongest tools that can be used for environmental protection, that is, legally enforceable
April 19, 1988

standards. Not all numbers related to environmental protection need to be standards, but not to have the option of using them is simply short-sighted and limits available tools for use in the future.
Pollution Probe has recommended that the authority to set standards should be added to Clause 8 wherever it is now limited to objective, guidelines, and codes of practice. Clearly, "objectives, guidelines, and codes of practice" are kind of fuzzy. They are subject to interpretation and abuse, if you like.
Elowever, when placed in law they become, if I can use the analogy, like a zoning by-law in a municipality. In order to change them one must go through a set process. If any government wanted to change those standards, to make them either stronger or weaker, it would have to come before this Parliament to do so. It would require a Bill and the kind of public notification and public debate that is occurring with regard to this Bill today. I think it is important that we provide that level of protection for our environment to ensure that any changes over and above those provided for by this Act must come before this House in order that the public is made aware of the changes desired.
The Bill should provide the opportunity to set numeric standards for ambient environmental quality, discharge limitations, or any other area which can be appropriately regulated in this manner and delete the reference to guidelines since they would allow for displacement of truly enforceable regulatory tools.
Also, codes of practice should not be part of the Department's legislative mandate. The development of such codes may be an internal tool for regulated parties to achieve compliance but should not replace regulatory or legal requirements.
I think it makes eminent sense that this amendment be accepted. It provides the Bill with stronger teeth and much more rigid adherence to the protection of our environment.

Madam Speaker, I understand that the time I have is somewhat limited. I will therefore try to state concisely why I agree with my colleagues that this provision in Section 2 of the Act is a cop-out compared to the language found in the proposed Environmental Protection Act which was circulated by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) some time ago.
Section (b) of the discussion paper which was circulated to interested parties throughout the country said that the Department's responsibilities were to include providing leadership-and I stress the word "leadership"-in the establishment of nationally consistent standards of environmental quality. I think that the word which should be stressed in the second part of this objective is "standard".
The legislation which we are studying today as amended by the legislative committee talks about the responsibility of the
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
department to establish nationally consistent levels of environmental quality. Therefore, I say it is a cop-out because, first, the word "leadership" has been removed. Quite clearly the Government does not want to take the bold step of saying that leadership should be part of its role as a national government.
The Government is not prepared to say that it should be the role of the Parliament of Canada and agencies of this Parliament and the national Government to speak for all of Canada and provide national leadership which can only come from a body that speaks for the whole of the country.
We are familiar with the Meech Lake agreement. As my colleague, the Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) has described it, the Meech Lake virus has found its way into the area of environmental protection. Quite clearly, the Government is reluctant to express it in those kinds of terms. It is reluctant to assume leadership. Again, I think this is reflected in the change of the word "standards" to ''levels", whatever "levels" means.
I recall Professor A1 Johnston who appeared before the joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate. He referred to the significance of the word "standard". He related it to the Canada Health Act which contains objectives to promote the health and well-being of Canadians, but then lists a set of standards which include such things as accessibility, universality, and comprehensiveness of a national health care plan with which the federal Government requires the provinces to comply with in order not to be penalized financially under the Canada Health Act.
This is the kind of standard which should be included in the environmental protection Bill. I am not saying the federal Government should devise these standards and impose them without any form of consultation because clearly there should be consultation among all levels of government and all interested parties. However, at some point someone has to decide what is in the national interest and clearly that is the role of the Parliament of Canada and the federal department or agency.
I deplore the fact that these changes have been made to this legislation. They are clearly not just semantic differences. These differences reflect themselves in many of the provisions of this Bill which we will be addressing during this report stage. Therefore, I wish to support the amendment of my colleague, the Member for Davenport, who argues that Clause 2 should be amended by striking out the text we find in lines 19 and 20 at page 2 and adding that it is the role of the department to endeavour to establish national standards of environmental quality.

Motion No. 4.
That Bill C-74 be amended in Clause 2 by adding immediately after line 28
at page 2 the following:
'(j) endeavour to act expeditiously to assess whether substances in use in
Canada are toxic or capable of becoming toxic.'
Motion No. 14.
That Bill C-74 be amended by adding immediately after line 38 at page 10
the following:
'14. Where a substance has been specified on the Priority substance list for a period of five years and the Ministers have not yet assessed whether the substance is toxic or capable of becoming toxic, any person may file a notice of objection with the Minister requesting that a board of review be established under section 88.'
Motion No. 25
That Bill C-74 be amended in Clause 88 by adding immediately after line
35 at page 65 the following:
'(5) Where a person files with the Minister a notice of objection under subsection 13(2) in respect of failure to make a decision about whether a substance is toxic the Minister shall establish a board of review to inquire into whether the substance is toxic or capable of becoming toxic.'
She said: Madam Speaker, I simply want to explain the purpose of these three motions. They reflect the frustration that many of us felt at committee stage that the Government was not prepared to implement sufficiently strong measures and particularly to move expeditiously to review the toxic chemicals. If the Government could have given us firm guarantees in the legislation, these amendments would not have been necessary.
The first motion simply seeks to add a new clause which states that the Minister shall endeavour to act expeditiously to assess whether substances in use in Canada are toxic or
capable of becoming toxic. We were unable to get any specific time frame in the legislation, so this at least gives the Minister some direction to act expeditiously.
The problem has been caused by slow response. There are substances which for years have been known to be toxic. Experts have raised objections and environmental groups have protested. Yet there has been a long tedious period of review. It has taken years to get toxic chemicals placed on a list and banned. In some cases, the chemical has even gone out of production because of objections in other places. It has even taken a long time to have substances that are no longer manufactured thoroughly banned on account of their toxicity. This motion is an additional attempt to get the Minister to act expeditiously.
Motion No. 14 deals with this problem of time. Five years is a long time for the Government to investigate the toxic substances in question. In the case of frivolous objections, there is no need to proceed. The Bill cannot compel the Government to assess toxicity of substances specified on the priority substances list.
The Minister's representative said that it would be unrealistic and unreasonable to require that any substances be assessed within a particular time frame. Even 10 years was considered to be unreasonable. What I have done is propose an amendment so that at least people can object if there has been no action in five years. That seems to me the least we can do in the circumstances. The Bill gives too much discretion to the Minister. With this amendment the Minister could still take as long as he wished to decide which priority substances were toxic and the public would have the right to abort a review when more than five years had lapsed.
The third motion, Motion No. 25, is consequential on the previous motion. Where a person files with the Minister a notice of objection in respect of failure to make a decision about whether a substance is toxic, the Minister shall establish a board of review to inquire into whether the subject is toxic or not. That seems to me the least we can do in the circumstances.
We have here a Bill with procedures that are, frankly, quite cumbersome. Many people have pointed out how cumbersome these procedures are and how very long it takes under the existing procedures to get a substance ruled to be toxic and regulated or banned. The new procedure is actually a little more complicated. We fear it will be even more time consuming to get action on it. These are three amendments which simply give citizens a bit of a right to push, to require the Minister to act when five years has elapsed. This makes the Bill a little more realistic and a little easier to respond to the really serious concerns environmentalists have. I would hope the Government would see fit at this stage to support these very reasonable and quite simple amendments.

Motion No. 6:
That Bill C-74 be amended by deleting Clause 5 and substituting the following therefor:

That Bill C-74 be amended by adding immediately after line 39 at page 5 the following:

Madam Speaker, I will speak briefly on Motion No. 6 and Motion No. 8. I would like to draw to the attention of my colleagues in this House the way in which Clause 5 is presently written. It does not indicate the disposition on the part of the Government of the day or the Minister of the day to appoint an advisory committee that would be balanced in representing different interests in the community at large. It may well be that that might happen, but it may not. It may well be that an advisory committee could be loaded, so to speak, in favour of one interest in society as opposed to another.
1 submit that it is good legislative practice to indicate in the law how a committee ought to be representative of the

April 19, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
community at large. This is the reason why in the amendment that Your Honour just read reference is made on the part of my Party to equal representation by industry, labour and nongovernmental groups, mainly public interest groups that are active in environmental protection.
Why is that? First, it is to ensure that there is a certain balance in advisory committees to be created under the clause. Second, it is to open up the process, to ensure that the process of environmental advisory committees, which committees would advise the Minister of the day, would have access to it as well as a guarantee in the legislation to have this type of access.
It was our Party which in committee ensured by way of an amendment the inclusion of labour in a clause further on in the Bill, an inclusion which had been omitted, so that it would be a participant in a consultative process envisaged further on in the Bill. We therefore spoke for labour on that occasion. We are glad to do the same here now by way of an amendment that opens up the process to these three major sectors in society which usually have something very important to say when it comes to environmental matters.
With respect to Motion No. 8, the purpose of the motion is very simple. It is to make public the information that is the object of Clause 6. It is a very straightforward amendment that endeavours to do something that we do in a variety of ways when it comes to reports in other activities that are of public interest.
Therefore I hope that the House will see fit to adopt Motion No. 6 and Motion No. 8 in order to improve the quality of the Bill, the quality of consultation and the quality of public information.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support Motion No. 6 put forward by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). I think it is an important matter to have in the type of consultations proposed here an advisory council composed of equal representation from industry, labour and environmental public interest groups. It would have the function of providing advice to the Minister on matters brought forward, make recommendations concerning administration of the Act and recommendations respecting biotechnology and products of biotechnology, and review the new chemicals program and report annually.
These same three groups, industry, labour and environmental, have been working together in a variety of respects. Apropos toxic chemicals they came forward with a united approach as to how they should be dealt with. So we have had some useful experience of the groups working together to try to come up with some decent standards and advice. It seems to me that this is a very reasonable proposal. Perhaps these groups have other ways of getting their advice into Government and felt that a permanent advisory council was necessary and that Government was not listening to them. They wanted to have some input on the over-all direction with respect to
how we are going and whether or not it is working. Frankly, we have a process that is not all that strong, and perhaps there need to be reviews of it. I do not mean solely with respect to particular substances where there can be input on the whole direction of the program to reduce pollution by toxic chemicals. There has been significant demand in order to have this type of a central consultative committee.
The second part of the proposal, Motion No. 8, I am a little bit more leery of because this is a federal-provincial advisory committee to advise Ministers on the exercise of powers. What makes me a little bit leery-and of course I am in favour of the principle of consultation between the federal and provincial Governments-is the very cumbersome process that has been put up. It is something like the double-whammy approach. First, we were told that if we were to have national standards with consultation then that was one thing. If a process of equivalency is set up that says that we will not have national standards, that we will let the provinces set up equivalent standards, and we will only have very modest guidelines, then why would there be the consultative process? It seems that one would spend all one's time consulting and that one would not end up with national standards since they have been rejected.
I am not happy with this. It seems that the principle of consultation is certainly a proper one. However, when we end up with too much consultation and we do not end up with adequate standards as a result of that consultation, I wonder if we are not wasting some time and should be going one or other route more consistently.
The third of the motions is the one that I proposed. It is Motion No. 9. It would amend the Bill to the effect that the Minister will make public all correspondence, documents and information arising from the work of the committees referred to in Sections 5 and 6, that is, the labour, industry and environmental committee, and the federal-provincial committee.
The reason for this needs to be understood very carefully. We have a Government that has bowed to pressure from the provinces to be consulted before the federal Government exercises its authority in environmental matters. This consultation seems to be going on at all times with respect to equivalency. It is being built into the process. However, there are some dangers in this consultation that have to be understood. One of them is a loophole that exists in accessing information passed between federal and provincial Governments. The provinces should not be able to become lobbyists in secret. By giving the public clear access to federal-provincial correspondence, abuse of this federal-provincial advisory process will be mitigated.
If we are to have the process which is proposed in the second motion, then it is very clear that experts, environmental groups and critics in the Opposition will be able to have access to the documents to ensure that there are not secret deals being made. We need to know what this advice is. Clearly, the environment is an area of shared jurisdiction in our Constitution. Clearly, the provinces have an important role. Clearly,
April 19, 1988

the need for national standards and the national presence is also there.
If we are to have decent environmental regulation, then we have to understand what consultation is going on between the federal Government and the provinces. We need to know what advice is being given. If a province is advising that it wants a pollution ghetto, if it is asking for standards to be reduced or is trying to look for ways to get out of having adequate environmental protection, then we need to know that. We do not want to have secret deals. So it seems to me very reasonable that Motion No. 9 would be passed.
It would simply respect the intent of the Bill to improve environmental protection and to involve the public and environmental groups. The Government has built this into the Bill at various stages. It has certainly showed a willingness to work with environmental groups and, indeed, to benefit from the expertise, the knowledge and experience which environmental groups have. It seems to me that this would be a very logical extension of that principle. Accordingly, I hope that the Government will see fit to support these amendments.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as we begin discussing Motion No. 6 and Motion No. 8, I am going to ask if it is possible to divide Motion No. 6 and vote on each part separately. The first part relates to Clause 5(1), and the second part relates to Clause 5(2). Motion No. 8 relates to Clause 6. Might we vote on Clauses 6(1) and 6(2) separately?
First, I will speak to Motion No. 6. The Canadian Environmental Protection Act does in fact provide an effective framework for protecting the Canadian environment. The Act is designed to counter the increasing number of environmental and health threats afflicting the world around us.
The very drafting and formulation of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act was truly a national effort, because it is the culmination of extensive public consultations involving all three levels of Government, industry, labour, the university community, and citizens' groups. Indeed, it is the product of five years' work as experts joined together to grapple with the problems associated with toxic chemicals.
That consultative process is built into the very fabric of this Act. Citizens now have unprecedented rights of participation in helping to implement and enforce the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
Citizens can request that a substance be added to the priority substance list for assessment and possible controls. They can object to regulatory decisions by requesting that a board of review be established, and they can make representation before those boards. Canadians can petition the Minister of the Environment to investigate an alleged infraction under the Act. The people of Canada will have a very strong say in how this Act is administered.
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
Section 5 of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act also provides the Minister with an opportunity to establish special advisory committees. It is an important provision; environmental concerns are complex. A Minister must have proper recourse to a range of possibilities in overseeing an implementation of the Act. Flexibility of approach is the key to good management.
The Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) has proposed that Section 5 be amended. He suggested that it require the Minister to establish an advisory council to oversee the administration of the Act. I find this point redundant. We have debated this extensively in committee. There already exists an advisory body, the Canadian Environmental Advisory Council, which advises the Minister. It was established in 1972.
The council provides guidance and makes recommendations to the Minister of the Environment, and through him to the Government as a whole, and through the Government to the public on environmental policy. Its work is becoming increasingly public. In the same manner as it was active in the national consultation process on CEPA and gave impetus to many of the changes in the earlier parts, so also will it play a key role in advising on the administration of the legislation following passage.
The council has been involved in the development of CEPA. It is now working on a project to enhance the efficiency of the assessment of substances. The council is representative; its members appointed to reflect the reality that is Canada. They come from all regions. At different times, the council members have been drawn from the ranks of academe, citizens' groups, industry, and labour, the goal being a genuine cross-section of Canadian society and expertise.
I see no point in the Hon. Member's amendment to tie down in legislation a reality that already exists, an advisory council to advise the Minister. In this section, with your indulgence, Madam Speaker, I do recommend that the House reject the first part of this amendment.
In regard to part (2) requiring an annual report on the activities of advisory committees, because Section 5 talks about advisory committees, the Government accepts that part of the motion if it refers to advisory committees.
In relation to Motion No. 8 before the House, we would also seek your indulgence, Madam Speaker, in having the two parts voted on separately. In this motion, Bill C-74 provides a Canada-wide framework of environmental protection. Forging a partnership between the federal Government and the provinces will serve to harmonize environmental controls, and ensure an equivalent level of protection for all Canadians, no matter where they reside in this country. The federal-provincial advisory committee is an important manifestation of that partnership. Therefore, it shall be established.
The committee's focus is regulations. The motion suggests that the committee also deal with monitoring activities

April 19, 1988
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
described in Clause 7. There is well-established co-operation among Governments for sharing monitoring and operating equipment, and Clause 7(2) confirms that. In our view, it is unnecessary to have this activity be the subject of a federal-provincial advisory committee.
The motion proposes the committee deal with clause 32 which establishes a list of toxic substances. This clause is linked with the regulation making power set in Clause 33, and regulations are the subject of the committee. The amendment is therefore not considered necessary. The amendment drops the whole idea of consultation in paragraph 33(1 )(c) which deals with regulations on the release of toxic substances to the environment at the commercial, manufacturing, or processing stages of the life cycle.
This paragraph will be of just as much interest and import to the provinces as paragraphs 33(1 )(a),(b), and (d) which also deal with regulations on the release of toxic substances. These areas have traditionally fallen within the purview of provincial governments.
In general, the motion would define a very narrow role for the federal-provincial advisory committee, while removing the flexibility to assign to it tasks of mutual interest to both the federal and provincial Governments. Rather, our intention is that the committee will be an important mechanism for forging and maintaining the federal-provincial partnership.
To be effective in this role, both the Minister and the committee must retain a considerable flexibility in the tasks which can be assigned and assumed. Therefore, Madam Speaker, we reject the first part of this motion. If, in any given year, the committee is active and contributes to the administration of the Act, its work must be included in the annual report to Parliament. Therefore, we accept the second part of this motion.
Motion No. 9 is aimed at releasing the maximum amount of information to the public on matters arising from the work of the ministerial and federal-provincial advisory committees established under Bill C-74. Section 5(2) of the Act already provides for public release of reports of the ministerial advisory committees, subject to the confidentiality provisions of the Act. This provision is necessary to allow ministerial advisory committees to work with confidential business information, such as trade secrets, where circumstances warrant.
As far the federal-provincial advisory committees are concerned, the Access to Information Act allows exemption from release for information transmitted between the two levels of Government. The motion as proposed might put in jeopardy the provision of advice to the Minister by the provinces, and therefore Motion No. 9 would not be supported by the Government.

Madam Speaker, I want to deal with Motion No. 6 at the outset. Motion No. 6
amends Bill C-74 by deleting Clause 5 and substituting the following:
Motion No. 6
"5.(1) For the purposes of carrying out the Minister's duties under this Act, the Minister shall establish an advisory council, composed of equal representation from industry, labour and environmental public interest groups,
It goes on to outline what the responsibilities of these groups would be; namely, to:
(a)	provide advice to the Minister on matters that have been brought to its attention or referred to it concerning notification, assessment or procedure, and policy issues;
That is the provision of advice. Then to:
(b)	make recommendations to the Minister concerning the administration of the Act;
So we are now talking about advice and recommendations. We go on to:
(c)	make recommendations with respect to biotechnology and products of biotechnology;
Lord only knows we certainly need some concrete recommendations in this new and evolving technology. Last to:
(d)	review the new chemicals program every three years.
We know how quickly we are changing in this new and dynamic field and certainly the review every three years just makes quite logical sense of chemical programs. Then we come to:
(2) The advisory council shall report annually to the the Minister on its
activities,-
It strikes me that we are elected Members of this House, and that the Minister through his contacts carries his responsibilities further than that of an elected Member, but he is in a position to give real meaning to listening to the grass-roots, to listening to the professional organizations and to listening to those labour and industry groups actively involved in pursuing improvement in pollution and pollution control. They have already worked together as the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) and the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) have said. We know that the STOP group and La societe pour vaincre la pollution, S.V.P., are very important.
We enable national standards and we establish national standards. This should be a primary goal which I am sure the Minister would like to have so there would not be the sense of copping out or hiding-which surely the Minister does not want. In the establishment of national standards and having this advisory group enable us to establish those national standards, we will be giving real meaning to the intent behind this particular Bill. I would strongly suggest that if the Minister will consider this, it would be much appreciated by groups in society with respect to the goals that he has established for this Bill.
April 19, 1988

If you look to Motion No. 8, Madam Speaker, you will see that there is a move on the part of my colleague from Davenport involving the deletion of Clause 6. I think his point was well accepted by the Parliamentary Secretary. I read from the committee reports, issue No. 22 for March 3, the exchange between the Member, the Hon. Member for Vancouver- Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), Mr. Higgins, the expert and the Parliamentary Secretary. It is obvious they had a pleasant exchange but fundamentally the exchange is all about why we need this correction. Mr. Higgins said:

"The guidelines proposed in clause 8 are certainly the sorts of issues that advisory committees could deal with to advise the minister."
I do not see why the Minister would not agree to be advised. I believe that he has very effective advisors, but this would add to his competence in the subject.
Later, my colleague said, "Given Mr. Higgins' answer, it would be desirable to move a subamendment to clause 6 by adding after the words" other environmental matters that are of mutual interest to the federal and provincial governments and pertain to this Act."

What we have here is a tidying up of a lot of rhetoric, an establishment of principle and practice that is clear, unfuzzy and denotes the goals that are envisaged in this Bill.

So I suggest that we adopt the effective and enlightened recommendations to improve the contents of this Bill and the procedures provided therein.

Motion No. 12.
That Bill C-74 be amended in Clause 11 by striking out line 16 at page 9
and substituting the following therefor:
"human, animal or plant life depends; or".
Motion No. 13.
That Bill C-74 be amended in Clause 11 by striking out line 18 at page 9
and substituting the following therefor:

She said: Madam Speaker, I rise to explain Motions Nos. 12 and 13 and to urge Hon. Members to support them. The purpose of these motions is to ensure that we have an adequately broad definition of the environment and of the kinds of harm that exist.
Clause 11 deals with toxic substances. It provides that for the purposes of this part, a substance is toxic if it is entering or may enter the environment in a quantity or concentration or under conditions, and the first condition is having or may have an immediate or long-term harmful effect on the environment. The second is constituting or that may constitute a danger to the environment on which human life depends. The third part says "constituting or that may constitute a danger in Canada to human life or health."
Under the first amendment at line 16 the new wording would be:
constituting or that may constitute a danger to the environment on which
human life depends;
Then the words "human life" simply become "life". This is to broaden the definition in two particular places and the point is to indicate very clearly that we are all part of the environment. It is not just human life and health that can be affected by toxic substances. We want to make it very clear that our
April 19, 1988

environment includes plants and animals, and if a toxic substance is causing harm to plants and animals, eventually it will get to us because we live on the same planet. There is a food chain, one thing leads to another, and the effect of toxic substances is magnified as they move up the food chain. If it is only lichens or very simple forms of life affected first, we should not ignore it on the grounds they are not human beings but some kind of low, non-conscious form of life. Lichens, after all, are eaten by other creatures, those creatures are eaten by larger creatures, and so on. Toxic substances are then concentrated as they move up the food chain.
I hope people will not see this as being unduly sentimental. I happen to take a perhaps more religious view of our responsibilities as stewards of the environment. However, we have to be practical. We all live on the planet and these things are connected. It is just foolish to think that we human beings stand at the top and we can ignore the threat to those beings further down the chain. We are all in it together and we have responsibilities. We have not taken those responsibilities very well and we have had all kinds of environmental disasters as a result of our lack of conscience, vigour, enforcement, and slowness in appreciating what is happening to the environment.
These amendments are to say let us be careful that we are not too narrow in defining only threats to human health or the environment on which human beings depend, but really understand that plants, animals and human beings all affect each other. We have to be clear. This is an Environmental Protection Act. Human health is an important part but let us not focus too narrowly and assume that by doing that we are going to protect ourselves or the environment.
It seems to me that these are simple amendments and will be recognized by every environmentalist as being eminently practical and wise. We cannot set ourselves apart and protect only ourselves. We have to be good environmentalists and understand the importance of protecting all life, plant and animal, and those of us who rise and speak in Parliament as well.

Madam Speaker, in support of this amendment I would like to bring to your attention the fact that we spent a considerable amount of time in committee debating this clause because it deals with a definition of nothing less than toxic substances. Therefore, this is the heart and soul, in a way, of this Bill. Toxic substances cannot be regulated, you will appreciate, until a comprehensive and adequate definition has been worked out. We spent a lot of time in committee focusing on two words, "significant" and "important". In the end we collectively managed to arrive at a significantly improved definition, the one here before us today. In that respect we were all quite satisfied that we had made progress.
The two motions deal with two other subclauses that were, in retrospect, overlooked at bit because of our preoccupation in
Canadian Environmental Protection Act
committee, as I recall it, with the first half of this clause. The thrust of the motion by the Hon. Member is to broaden the orientation of this clause from just and only the human perspective, as she put it, to a recognition of the totality of the value of an environment which is more than just humans. We know that what happens in animal life, for example, and this is why we have the Canadian Wildlife Service, or in plant life, eventually can reach humans because of the ecological chain the Hon. Member spoke about. If this clause is left the way it reads now, it means that toxic substances are important only within the context of human life. That is not bad. It is a good start.
However, we are saying, in the hope the Parliamentary Secretary will agree, that there has to be a totality in the description of what is toxic which is broader than just what affects humans. Hence, the value and importance of this amendment which also looks at life as plants and the animal world, not because of a romantic notion so much, as the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) quite rightly put it, but because we know from experience that what happens in animals and plant life eventually has a significant, and sometimes profound effect on human beings on this planet.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will be very brief. I would like to point out that what has happened here today was generally the kind of thing that happened in the committee. There was a kind of co-operation that took place with respect to the seven or eight amendments that we have discussed here today. The Government accepted three of them and is taking a look at two others.
However, in relation to Motion No. 12 and Motion No. 13, we feel they are not necessary and the Government will not support them. They are designed to add the concept of animal and plant life, but subclause 11 (a) deals with the effects on the environment. If you go to Clause 3 of the Bill where it defines "environment", it already includes plant and animal life in the words "living organisms" in the definition of the word "environment". We believe these amendments are therefore unnecessary and the Government will not support them.

He said: Madam Speaker, I find myself in a somewhat unorthodox situation and I will explain why. This Bill is very important to me and I would like to expand upon it. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   BLUE WATER BRIDGE AUTHORITY ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Consequently, I do not feel that it would be right for me to continue as the sponsor of this Bill. I have been in contact with my colleague, the Member for Kent (Mr. Hardey) who will take over for me as the sponsor of this Bill.
I would like to take this opportunity, however, to say a few words because 1 am honoured to have been given the opportunity to present this Bill. The concerns which have been expressed to me centre around the issue of liability on the Blue Water Bridge which spans the St. Clair River between Michigan and Ontario.
As Hon. Members may recall, the insurance industry has been very volatile in recent years and liability insurance costs sky-rocketed. In 1984-85 the Blue Water Bridge Authority's insurance brokers provided a $50 million public liability umbrella policy on the bridge for $18,000 a year. In 1986-87 the highest insurance package that the brokers could offer was a $45 million public liability policy for $80,000 a year-a decrease in coverage with a premium increase of nearly 500 per cent.
Traffic on the bridge continues to increase dramatically. The commissioners and the general manager of the Blue Water Bridge Authority are concerned that, in the event of a major disaster on the bridge, their personal property and possessions could be attached if the $50 million coverage was not sufficient. Given the liberal insurance settlements we have seen recently in the courts, this is a real concern.
It is the contention of the Department of Transport that this issue is dealt with through the common law and is covered through other Acts of Parliament. I am aware of Transport Canada's concern and I do respect the department's position. However, I have been approached by the Blue Water Bridge Authority and it is clear that the commissioners do not feel entirely comfortable with the department's position.
I believe that the concerns expressed by the Blue Water Bridge Authority are valid. Also, I do understand and respect
the reservations of the Department of Transport. However, the problem remains and a solution must be found. It is my feeling that a legislative committee will provide the best possible forum in which to resolve this subject to everyone's satisfaction.
It may be that the solution to the issue lies somewhere between Bill C-210 and the current situation. I would encourage all Hon. Members to support this Bill at second reading. It is too important a subject to ignore.
I understand that consultations have taken place with the opposition Parties and I believe, Madam Speaker, that you will find consent for the following motion:

Authority Act, be, by unanimous consent, amended to stand in the name of

Madam
Speaker, I just want to make one short intervention. I appreciate that we want to get Bill C-210 into a legislative committee so that there can be an examination of both its principle and its content. However, I have one question in my mind after having read the Bill. The Bill says that the members of the bridge authority are not personally liable for any injury or loss suffered by any user of the Blue Water Bridge as a result of an act of terrorism or the fault, neglect, want of skill, or willful or wrongful act of any person.
Does that free the board as an entity from any action taken against it because of a decision it has made? I am not sure that it was the intent of the mover to take away the legal responsibility and liability of the board should it decide to forego maintenance and should that lack of maintenance lead to a situation which creates an accident. I do not think that the board should be exempt from action by a citizen who finds himself injured because of that.

I hope that that will be examined during the discussions of the legislative committee to ensure that while an individual member is not taken to court as a result of an action over which he or she had no control, there must be some onus on the board itself. If a court of law finds the board negligent, an aggrieved party should have some recourse such as a pay-out or whatever.
We are not going to put up any more speakers and are quite willing to have this Bill passed very quickly.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   BLUE WATER BRIDGE AUTHORITY ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I only want a moment or two to participate in this debate. I certainly have no intention of delaying this Bill in any way, shape, or form. I share the concerns which have been brought to the attention of the House. Perhaps, with unanimous consent, the Member could speak again and address some of those concerns. I would be willing to give such consent.
We do not want, of course, board members to be singularly or collectively responsible for liability. On the other hand, there must be provision, in the event of a mishap, for persons affected to collect. For example, if there was a major spill from a vehicle that perhaps ran off the end of the bridge due to a deficiency in the bridge as opposed to their own neglect, we would want to ensure there are provisions there for that kind of situation.
The Member prepared a briefing book for us and it states in the notes that he was to have delivered to us prior to his promotion, which cut down somewhat on his speech, that in the event of a major disaster on the bridge there is presently a $50 million liability coverage. If I understand it correctly, the situation is such that board members could be sued for a claim that was in excess of that. That is essentially the problem that the Hon. Member was explaining to us.
Nevertheless, we are also concerned particularly because of settlements that have been made in courts in recent years. We do not want to create the situation which would cause undue hardship for members of the board of that bridge authority.
We are willing to let the Bill go to committee. I invite the Member or one of his colleagues to perhaps answer some of those concerns. If that is possible, as far as I am concerned the Bill could then go to a legislative committee in order to be dealt with as soon as possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   BLUE WATER BRIDGE AUTHORITY ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is an honour to rise on behalf of the Government and present its view on this Private Members' Bill. First, I want to commend my colleague, the Member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. James), for his appointment as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services. It is a very important department which will involve a lot of extra work on his behalf. I am sure his
Blue Water Bridge Authority Act
constituents will understand that and will be thankful that he is to provide his judgment on behalf of the people of Canada.
Second, I want to commend the Hon. Member for this Bill. My colleague is a new Member and does not remember the old days when private Members had a Private Members' Hour but their Bills were almost universally talked out. No matter what Government was in power, private Members had no ability to legislate. This built frustrations that were genuine on our part as back-benchers.
Therefore, this new procedure whereby more and more Bills go to legislative committee and can actually become law of the land is a tremendous addition to law-making in this country. There is now a short list of 20 Bills which can come up, six of which can be drawn and are actually forced to a vote. Even though a Member may have a Bill that is inconvenient or indeed opposed by the Cabinet, if it is on the votable list it will come to a vote and the Cabinet has to accept that. That is tremendous power for back-benchers.
It is an historic occasion for a Bill to go to a legislative committee. We should be thankful because this would not be the rule of the House if it had not been for the actions of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). Only he had the courage, after a whole succession of Prime Ministers, to face this directly. As a new Prime Minister he said that he wanted Members of Parliament to be important. We should all be thankful for that. We may have partisan differences, but the Prime Minister deserves credit for this amendment to our rules.
In response to the Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus) and the Member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell (Mr. Boudria), I have seen a briefing note raising the points the officials have made. I think it would be wiser to send the Bill to committee where we will make sure all the witnesses necessary will explain any questions Members might have. I suggest that would be a wiser resolution, rather than getting into debate on it today. Therefore, I hope Members will agree to send it to committee.
